# agent-snap

Product name: **Blink**. Implementation name: **agent-snap**. [`docs/NAMESPACE.md`](docs/NAMESPACE.md) is the published migration policy, and it keeps every shipped name.

Blink records zero-impact Git working-tree checkpoints for AI agent sessions. Spec and phased roadmap:

- `docs/BLINK_SPEC.md`
- `docs/BLINK_DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md`

Identity is frozen: executable `agent-snap`, packages `@agent-snap/*`, JSONL methods as shipped, refs under `refs/agent-snapshots/`. Do not rename, dual-write, or migrate those identifiers. [`docs/NAMESPACE.md`](docs/NAMESPACE.md) records why, and what a later rename needs first.

## Safety invariants

These are non-negotiable. Capture, list, and inspect must never modify `HEAD`, the real index, normal refs, or the working tree.

- Snapshot creation uses a private scratch `GIT_INDEX_FILE` outside the repository. Fail closed if that cannot be guaranteed.
- A restore plan and a restore also set `GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY` to a private object directory beside their scratch index, whose `info/alternates` names the real object directory. Neither writes the real object store.
- A restore (FR-16) writes working-tree files only through `read-tree -m -u` on the scratch index that its own fresh capture filled, after it recomputes the plan from that capture. It never writes the real index, `HEAD`, or refs, and Blink's only file in the Git directory is the restore lock. What the repository's smudge and process filters write is outside this rule. Only `serve --restore` and the CLI `restore` command run it.
- Every Git command of a restore that sets `GIT_INDEX_FILE` pins `core.splitIndex=false`. Every Git command of a restore's captures and its write also pins `core.trustctime=true`, `core.checkStat=default`, `core.ignoreStat=false`, `core.fsmonitor=` with an empty value, `core.sparseCheckout=false`, `checkout.workers=1`, and `core.hooksPath` to an empty scratch directory, and `hook.<name>.enabled=false` for each configured hook. Every other Git command of a restore from step 5 on pins `core.hooksPath`, `core.fsmonitor=`, and the hook settings, and the read that finds the `sparse_checkout` blocker never carries the sparse pin. `snapshot.create` and a restore plan's capture never take the eight pins, because the sparse pin changes their tree. The hook settings include `hook.post-index-change.enabled=false`. Every Git command of a capture, a restore plan, and a restore sets `GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS=1`. Those that a plan and a restore run in the real repository pass the resolved `--git-dir` and `--work-tree`, except a restore's commands before step 5. The commands in a plan's evidence repository keep that repository's environment, so a partial clone never fetches into the real object store. T is the lock file's change time in whole seconds, taken right after the core writes the lock line, and never its modification time, which any process can set back. The core refuses unless setting the modification time back to 1,000,000,000 leaves the change time later than that and at or after T. Before the write, the core judges each planned path on the stat that the capture recorded in the scratch index, never on the disk. It refuses one recorded on another device than the lock file, and one recorded with a change time at or after T's second and a modification time before it. Right before the write, the core sets the scratch index's modification time to T, reads it back, and refuses unless it reads T. T is never 0. Each of these rules closes a case in which a probe saw Git overwrite an edit made after the capture, or write outside the plan, with exit `0`.
- The pins fix the settings that would weaken the write. Any other configuration change between a restore's capture and its write refuses the restore, through a fingerprint of `git config --list -z --show-scope --show-origin` read with no `-c` setting. Do not answer a new setting with a new pin unless it weakens the write at its standing value.
- Git's check before the write is not a complete guard. An edit to a planned path after Git checked it and before Git writes it is overwritten. The rules above keep that window as short as Git's own checkout keeps it. Never widen it, for example by making every index entry racy.
- On POSIX, a restore's write and each Git command of the capture after it start in a new session, and no other Git command of a restore does. The write's Git has no pipe to the core and inherits the restore lock's descriptor, which no other child receives. The core ends the lock with `LOCK_UN`, never by close alone. Terminal and guardian group signals must never reach these Git commands. Windows restore stays refused until CI proves its equivalent.
- `SnapClient` keeps a frozen copy of `serveArgs` and refuses an element that names the restore entry at construction and at every spawn. `SnapClient.request` refuses a method that is not a primitive string and the method `snapshot.restore`. Only `SnapClient.restore` and the support check of `confirmRestore` spawn `serve --restore`.
- Every Git invocation strips inherited `GIT_*` repository-redirect variables and runs against the resolved repo. The exceptions are `Store.Diff` and the reads of a restore plan that run in its own evidence repository, including those of the plan that a restore recomputes at step 8. Each runs Git in a private bare evidence repository outside the worktree whose only link to the resolved repo is a read-only `objects/info/alternates` entry, so attributes, configuration, and replace refs cannot shape the evidence, and a missing blob in a partial clone fails there instead of fetching into the real object store. The plan's capture and its reads of the worktree and the real index run in the resolved repo and stay under the rule.
- `Store` owns every hidden-ref path. Callers never construct `refs/agent-snapshots/...` themselves.
- Host plugins and extensions never invoke Git and never spawn `agent-snap` except through `SnapClient`.
- Any operation that would write working-tree files needs a dedicated design review, adversarial tests, and explicit user confirmation UX that lifecycle hooks cannot manufacture.
- Timeout, cancellation, teardown, and concurrency fail closed. A timed-out create must not produce an unobserved checkpoint.
- A restore honors cancellation and timeout until its last check before the write. From then until its answer is written, the core discards stop signals, runs on a context that cannot be cancelled, and never signals its Git. In `serve --restore`, the end of standard input cancels a `snapshot.restore` in flight like a signal and never cancels a `ping`, and a cancel never drops a request line that was read. No client or guardian path sends `SIGKILL` to a restore after the moment before its request is written. Once the write's Git starts, the restore answers with a result and never with an error, and the code after the process start has no error return. The core logs a cleanup failure after that start, and the failure never changes the outcome. A caller is never told that nothing changed when files may have changed, and no message describes a result as writing nothing.
- Public protocol results are runtime-validated at the TypeScript boundary before they reach a host.

## Architecture

```text
OpenCode plugin ─┐
                 ├─ packages/core SnapClient ─ JSONL stdin/stdout ─ cmd/agent-snap
Pi extension ────┘         │                         │
                           │                         ├─ internal/protocol
                           │                         └─ internal/snapshot ─ Git plumbing
                           └─ coalesce + process teardown
```

| Layer | Owns |
| --- | --- |
| `cmd/agent-snap` | CLI parsing and process entry. No Git policy. |
| `internal/protocol` | Strict JSONL parse, unknown-key rejection, dispatch, error codes. |
| `internal/snapshot` | Repo discovery, scratch index, hidden refs, dedup, list/get, diff evidence repository. |
| `packages/core` | Typed client, result validation, cancellation, process-tree teardown. |
| `packages/opencode`, `packages/pi` | Host lifecycle and tools. No Git, no protocol parsing. |

New capability order: spec (`docs/BLINK_SPEC.md`) → `Store` → protocol → `types` / `SnapClient` validation → CLI → host tools last.

## How to plan a change

Before writing code, name all of:

1. Affected phase in `docs/BLINK_DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md`
2. Safety impact (read-only vs working-tree write)
3. Compatibility impact (CLI, JSONL, npm, refs)
4. API contract (request, result, errors, limits)
5. Test strategy
6. Release / rollback plan

Prioritize: safety and data-loss risk → reliability and cross-platform correctness → evidence and review quality → explicit restore → branding and packaging.

YAGNI: do not implement restore, retention/GC, or Blink renaming until that phase. Do not add a service layer, plugin framework, or generic repository for a single function.

DRY: put shared rules in the owning layer (`Store` for refs, `protocol` for validation, `SnapClient` for transport). Do not extract host formatters until a third consumer exists.

One concern per change set. Do not mix product renaming, restore writes, and process-safety work.

## Patterns that match this repo

Use a pattern only when it already fits the architecture:

- **Facade** — `snapshot.Store` is the only Git boundary.
- **Strict dispatcher** — `protocol.dispatch` is a closed method switch with exact error codes.
- **Port** — `SnapLike` exists so hosts can be tested without a subprocess.
- **Scheduler** — `createCoalescedScheduler` is the idle/settled burst policy.
- **Strategy** — POSIX process-group teardown vs Windows process-tree teardown, isolated in `packages/core/src/teardown.ts`.

Do not introduce a DI container, event bus, generic repository, ORM, or host-side Git wrapper.

## Code standards

Write structured, small, total functions. Prefer explicit data and control flow over cleverness. Names describe the domain (`Create`, `List`, `commitRefs`), not the mechanism (`handleData`, `processManager`).

Comments are reserved for non-obvious safety constraints (scratch-index placement, guardian teardown, CAS retries). Do not narrate what the next line does.

### Go

- Standard library only. A new module dependency needs an explicit, documented reason.
- Wrap errors with `fmt.Errorf("…: %w", err)` and keep the operation in the message.
- Reject unknown protocol keys, missing `cwd`, blank strings, and out-of-range limits. Do not coerce types.
- Tests live in the same package. Use real temporary Git repos for store tests; table-driven cases for protocol/CLI validation.
- Run `gofmt` and `go vet`. Match existing error-string and helper style (`git`, `testRepo`, `serveRequest`).

### TypeScript

- ESM. Bun is the toolchain: `bun install`, `bun run`, `bun test`. Tests use the `node:test` and `node:assert` APIs so the same files run on Bun and, through `bun run test:node`, on Node. No extra test or assertion framework.
- Published packages run on Node in Pi and on compiled Bun in OpenCode. `packages/*/src` uses `node:` APIs only, never Bun globals. In a compiled host `process.execPath` is the host's own CLI, so anything spawned from it must keep working there (`bun run smoke` checks this).
- Runtime-validate every RPC success and error payload. Never trust subprocess JSON.
- Honor `AbortSignal` and the default timeout. Teardown must be started on cancel or timeout.
- Keep `SnapLike` as the host dependency. Do not reach into `SnapClient` internals from plugins.
- Match existing formatting, imports, and file layout. Do not add comments that duplicate types or names.

### Performance

- Reuse one `SnapClient` transport while it is healthy. Do not spawn a core process per tool call.
- Coalesce bursty idle/settled events; do not snapshot on every host event.
- Deduplicate identical trees in `Store.Create`. Do not mint a commit when `reused` should be true.
- Bound protocol input (4 MiB line) and list limits (1–100). Diff pages are bounded by FR-14 (200 files, `max_patch_bytes` of hunks). Any new payload must define size and truncation before implementation.
- Scratch indexes are created outside the repo and removed on success and failure.

## Testing and verification

Required local gates:

```sh
test -z "$(gofmt -l .)"
go test ./...
go vet ./...
bun run build
bun run typecheck
bun run test
bun run test:node
go build -o bin/agent-snap ./cmd/agent-snap
AGENT_SNAP_BIN="$PWD/bin/agent-snap" bun run smoke
AGENT_SNAP_BIN="$PWD/bin/agent-snap" bun run pack-check
```

Cover empty history, invalid IDs, other-worktree refs, SHA-1 and SHA-256 repos, ignored/untracked/staged/unstaged files, symbolic-ref refusal, concurrent creates, cancellation, and malformed protocol responses when those paths exist.

Working-tree writes, if ever added, also need adversarial tests for dirty trees, deletions, renames, nested worktrees, cancellation, and failure between backup and write.

## Do not

- Rename protocol methods, packages, the executable, or ref namespaces without a published migration policy and compatibility tests.
- Expose raw Git commands through host plugins.
- Let lifecycle hooks create restore confirmations.
- Present an inference as a confirmed fact. Review findings must cite a path and hunk from a snapshot diff, in the FR-14 citation form.
- Commit secrets, or log repository file contents in diagnostics.
- Add dependencies, abstractions, or files that are not required by the current phase.

# Blink

Zero-impact Git working-tree snapshots for AI agent sessions.

Agent sessions mutate your working tree relentlessly. Blink records
snapshots of the working tree at key moments — session start (baseline) and
when the agent settles to idle — without ever touching `HEAD`, the real index,
or the working tree. Snapshots live in hidden git refs
(`refs/agent-snapshots/*`), so they survive `git gc`, never appear in `git
branch`, and never collide with your real history.

Blink ships as the `agent-snap` executable and the `@agent-snap/core`,
`@agent-snap/opencode`, and `@agent-snap/pi` packages. Those names, the JSONL
methods, and the `refs/agent-snapshots/` refs stay as they are, so an existing
configuration keeps working. [docs/NAMESPACE.md](docs/NAMESPACE.md) records
that decision, with install and rollback steps.

## How it works

1. A Go core (`cmd/agent-snap`) exposes `create` / `list` / `get` / `diff` / `restore-plan` / `ping` as
   direct JSON commands and a long-running JSONL `serve` mode on stdin/stdout.
2. Thin TypeScript adapters launch and reuse the Go subprocess:
   - `@agent-snap/opencode` — an OpenCode plugin (baseline at
     `session.created`, coalesced snapshot at `session.idle`, plus
     `agent_snap_create` / `agent_snap_list` / `agent_snap_get` /
     `agent_snap_diff` / `agent_snap_restore_plan` tools).
   - `@agent-snap/pi` — a Pi Coding Agent extension (baseline at
     `session_start`, coalesced snapshot at `agent_settled`, cleanup at
     `session_shutdown`, plus `agent_snap_create` / `agent_snap_list` /
     `agent_snap_get` / `agent_snap_diff` / `agent_snap_restore_plan` tools and
     `agent-snap-create` / `agent-snap-list` / `agent-snap-get` /
     `agent-snap-diff` commands).
3. Every create builds a tree from a **temporary index**
   (`GIT_INDEX_FILE` pointing at a scratch file), so the real index is never
   written. The commit is created with `git commit-tree` against hidden refs —
   `HEAD` never moves.
4. Unchanged trees are deduplicated: a create whose tree matches the latest
   snapshot simply reuses it (`reused: true`) instead of minting a commit.
5. Snapshot refs are namespaced per worktree (derived from the resolved git
   dir), so linked worktrees never collide; `latest` moves through an atomic
   `update-ref` compare-and-swap transaction, keeping the snapshot chain
   linear under concurrent creates.

## JSONL wire protocol

`agent-snap serve` reads JSON requests, one per line, from stdin and writes
one JSON response per line to stdout.

Request:

```json
{"id":1,"method":"snapshot.create","params":{"cwd":"/path/to/repo","reason":"why","source":"tool","host":"pi"}}
```

Response (success):

```json
{"id":1,"result":{"id":"20260814T120000.000000000Z-abc123def456","commit":"abc123def456","reason":"why","created_at":"2026-08-14T12:00:00Z","source":"tool","host":"pi","changed_files":["src/main.go"],"reused":false}}
```

Response (error — processing continues with the next request):

```json
{"id":1,"error":{"code":-32601,"message":"method not found"}}
```

Methods:

| Method           | Params                        | Result                                   |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `ping`           | —                             | `{"status":"ok","version":...}`          |
| `snapshot.create`| `cwd`, `reason?`, `source?`, `host?` | snapshot object (see above)       |
| `snapshot.list`  | `cwd`, `limit?`               | `{"snapshots":[...]}` (newest first)     |
| `snapshot.get`   | `cwd`, `id`                   | snapshot detail object                   |
| `snapshot.diff`  | `cwd`, `from`, `to`, `offset?`, `max_patch_bytes?` | one diff page            |
| `snapshot.restore_plan` | `cwd`, `id`, `paths?`, `offset?`, `current_tree?` | one restore plan page |

Error codes: `-32700` parse error, `-32601` method not found,
`-32602` invalid params, `-32603` internal error, `-32001` snapshot not found,
`-32002` stale restore plan.

`source` and `host` are the snapshot's origin: what asked for it, and which
integration sent the request. Each is a lowercase hyphenated token of at most
64 characters. They are stored in the snapshot commit and returned by create,
list, and get when present. The CLI records `source: cli`; the OpenCode and Pi
integrations record their own host and event. Origin is reported by the
caller, so treat it as a label, not evidence. No session identifiers are
stored. See FR-13 in [`docs/BLINK_SPEC.md`](docs/BLINK_SPEC.md).

`snapshot.diff` returns the changed files and hunks between two snapshots of
the same worktree, one page at a time: at most 200 files and 64 KiB of hunks
by default. Each file says whether its hunks are on the page (`full`,
`truncated`, `deferred`, or `binary`), and `next_offset` names the next page.
The same pair gives the same result with the same Git, because the diff runs
in a scratch repository that ignores Git attributes and configuration. See
FR-14 in [`docs/BLINK_SPEC.md`](docs/BLINK_SPEC.md).

`snapshot.restore_plan` lists what restoring a snapshot would do to the working
tree, one page at a time, and changes nothing. A request with `offset` above 0
must carry the `current_tree` from the first page. If the working tree no
longer captures to `current_tree`, the method answers `-32002`.

The CLI exposes the same plan as
`agent-snap restore-plan <id> [--cwd <dir>] [--path <path>]... [--offset <n>] [--current-tree <oid>]`.
`--path` may repeat, and with none the plan covers the whole tree. The command
exits `0` when it prints a plan, including one that is not applicable, and `1`
on any error, including a stale `--current-tree`.

`client.restorePlan(cwd, id, { paths?, offset?, currentTree? }, signal?)`
returns the validated restore plan (section 8.5). It rejects with
`SnapProtocolError` for a plan that breaks section 8.5, and with
`SnapRestorePlanUnsupportedError` (which extends `SnapRpcError`, code -32601)
when the installed `agent-snap` cannot plan restores. `SnapLike` gains
`restorePlan`.

`client.retentionReport(cwd, offset?, signal?)` returns one validated page of
the retention report (section 8.7). It rejects with `SnapProtocolError` for a
report that breaks section 8.7. It rejects with
`SnapRetentionReportUnsupportedError`, which extends `SnapRpcError` with code
-32601, when the installed `agent-snap` cannot report retention. `SnapLike`
gains `retentionReport`. See FR-17 in
[`docs/BLINK_SPEC.md`](docs/BLINK_SPEC.md).

Both hosts expose the plan as `agent_snap_restore_plan(id, paths?, offset?, current_tree?, cwd?)`.
The tool is read-only and returns one page as text. It names the `offset` and
`current_tree` to request next. No release can apply a restore. See FR-15 in
[`docs/BLINK_SPEC.md`](docs/BLINK_SPEC.md).

## Development

These local gates match CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`). `gofmt` is required;
CI runs the Go core on Linux, Windows, and macOS and prints each platform's
skipped Go tests with their reasons. It also runs TypeScript tests on Linux,
Windows, and macOS on both Bun and Node, and smoke on Linux and Windows. Use
`bun run test`, not `bun test`: the script builds first and raises Bun's 5 s
per-test timeout, which teardown tests exceed.

```sh
test -z "$(gofmt -l .)"
go test ./... && go vet ./...
bun install
bun run build && bun run typecheck && bun run test
bun run test:node                                          # core and Pi tests on Node, Pi's runtime
go build -o bin/agent-snap ./cmd/agent-snap
AGENT_SNAP_BIN="$PWD/bin/agent-snap" bun run smoke         # includes a compiled Bun host
AGENT_SNAP_BIN="$PWD/bin/agent-snap" bun run pack-check    # bun pm pack, npm install, check on Node and Bun
```

## Safety model

- Never moves `HEAD`, never writes the real index (a private temp dir holds
  the scratch `GIT_INDEX_FILE`), never writes to the working tree.
- Inherited git-repository environment (`GIT_DIR`, `GIT_WORK_TREE`,
  `GIT_INDEX_FILE`, `GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY`, …) is stripped from every git
  invocation, so commands are pinned to the resolved repository. A diff runs
  in a scratch bare repository outside the worktree that only reads the
  repository's objects, so attributes and configuration cannot change it.
- Commits are written to hidden refs only; no history rewrite, no branch
  updates.
- `git add -A` honors `.gitignore`; the snapshot tree is what the agent would
  commit.
- The TS client runtime-validates every child response, tears down the child
  process group on timeout or close (so a timed-out create can never produce
  a late snapshot), and respawns the transport lazily.

## Roadmap

- **Restore (`snapshot.restore`)** — deliberately out of scope for this MVP.
  Restoring means writing files into the working tree, which is a destructive
  operation that needs careful safety work (backup of current tree, staged
  vs. unstaged preservation, conflict handling, dry-run). Planned as a
  separate, fully safety-tested release.
- Snapshot garbage collection / retention policy.

# @agent-snap/core

Type-safe TypeScript client for Blink. It spawns the Blink core binary as
`agent-snap serve` and speaks the JSONL wire protocol over stdin/stdout:

```ts
import { SnapClient } from "@agent-snap/core"

const client = SnapClient.fromEnv() // honours AGENT_SNAP_BIN
const snap = await client.create("/path/to/repo", "before-refactor")
const items = await client.list("/path/to/repo", 10)
await client.close()
```

Safety properties:

- requests support `AbortSignal`; aborting (or a timeout) tears down the
  child process group — a cancelled create can never silently produce a late
  snapshot;
- on Unix the whole process group is signalled (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after
  a grace period); on Windows the child tree is killed via `taskkill /T /F`
  and cleanup fails closed unless taskkill succeeds *and* the root exits
  (see [docs/DIAGNOSTICS.md](../../docs/DIAGNOSTICS.md));
- `serveArgs` and `request` cannot reach the restore entry. The constructor
  copies `serveArgs` into a frozen array by index, calling no method of the
  caller's value, and throws a `TypeError` when an element starts with
  `restore` after its leading `-` characters. `request`
  rejects with a `TypeError` for a method that is not a primitive string and
  for `snapshot.restore`;
- responses are runtime-validated before being handed to the host;
- the client respawns the transport lazily after any crash or close.

# @agent-snap/opencode

Blink plugin for OpenCode 1.x (>= 1.18.18) and 2.x (>= 2.2.5). The package
name stays `@agent-snap/opencode`, so an existing OpenCode configuration keeps
working. See the repository README for full details.

- Baseline snapshot at `session.created` (promise tracked; failures are
  logged, never unhandled).
- Coalesced snapshot at `session.idle` (1.5 s burst window); `session.status`
  → `busy` cancels a pending idle snapshot and aborts one already in flight.
- `session.deleted` aborts in-flight work and forgets the session; idle for
  an unknown session is ignored (never falls back to the plugin directory).
- Events are rejected once the plugin starts closing; `dispose` is a shutdown
  barrier: flushes pending snapshots, aborts leftover work, and closes the Go
  subprocess.
- Tools: `agent_snap_create(reason?, cwd?)`, `agent_snap_list(cwd?, limit?)`,
  `agent_snap_get(id, cwd?)`,
  `agent_snap_diff(from, to, offset?, max_patch_bytes?, cwd?)`,
  `agent_snap_restore_plan(id, paths?, offset?, current_tree?, cwd?)`. Every
  tool honours the caller's abort signal. `agent_snap_diff` returns one page of Git
  evidence and names the `offset` of the next page.
  `agent_snap_restore_plan` returns one page of a read-only restore plan,
  names the `offset` and `current_tree` of the next page, and changes
  nothing. This release cannot apply a restore. Tool text prints a path, a
  reason, or an origin value in double quotes with C escapes when it holds a
  control character, a double quote, or a backslash, so a file name cannot
  forge a line.
- Every snapshot records host `opencode` and source `session-start`,
  `session-idle`, or `tool`. No session identifier is stored.

Enable in `opencode.json(c)`:

```jsonc
// OpenCode 2.x
{ "plugins": ["@agent-snap/opencode"] }

// OpenCode 1.x
{ "plugin": ["@agent-snap/opencode"] }
```

The entry's default export carries `server` for 1.x and `setup` for 2.x;
each host imports only its own adapter. On 2.x, tools that omit `cwd` use the
calling session's directory.

Set `AGENT_SNAP_BIN` if the `agent-snap` binary is not on `PATH`.

# Changelog

## Unreleased

- A linked worktree added under a removed worktree's name no longer inherits
  that worktree's snapshots. `snapshot.list` leaves them out,
  `snapshot.get`, `snapshot.diff`, and `snapshot.restore_plan` answer `-32001`
  for them, and `snapshot.create` neither reuses them nor chains onto them.
  Before, a restore plan could target the removed worktree's work. A worktree's
  timeline starts at the modification time of its `commondir` file (FR-4). No
  ref, namespace, or protocol field changes, and the old refs stay until a
  person drops the namespace.
- `snapshot.restore_plan` blocks a written path (a create, modify, or type
  change) as `name_collision` when the working tree folds case and a parent
  directory of the path exists on disk only under a spelling that differs by
  case, such as a `Dir/` that holds an ignored file where the snapshot has
  `dir/y`. The restore keeps that directory, and Git writes the file into it as
  `Dir/y`, so a capture afterwards differs from `result_tree`. Before, the plan
  was applicable. When `core.ignorecase` is true, a parent does not block if
  the result tree holds a path below it that `HEAD` also holds, because a
  capture then keeps the result tree's spelling. When `core.ignorecase` is false
  on a volume that folds case, that exemption does not apply, because Git then
  records the disk spelling. A directory that the restore empties does not
  block.
  The plan lists the names in each directory once and never follows a symbolic
  link. A directory it cannot read puts the path in the way. This is the second
  rule of `name_collision` in FR-15.
- `snapshot.restore_plan` blocks a `delete` as `name_collision` when
  `core.ignorecase` is true, the working tree folds case, and the delete takes
  the last `HEAD` path that kept a parent's spelling. An example is `HEAD`
  `dir/a` with an untracked `dir/q` that the restore keeps while the disk spells
  the directory `Dir/`. A capture after the restore records `Dir/q`, so it
  differs from `result_tree`. A directory counts as kept when the restore
  only rewrites a path below it, as in a delete of `dir/a` beside a modify of
  `dir/q`. Git rewrites a changed file in place and removes a directory only
  after its deletes leave it empty. It also blocks a written path as
  `untracked_in_the_way` when `core.ignorecase` is false and the volume
  resolves the path, or a parent of it, to a current-tree path under another
  spelling. Examples are a case-only rename of `Readme` to `README`, and a
  symbolic link `Dir` where the snapshot has `dir/y`. Git then matches the
  paths it removes by bytes, finds an untracked file in the way, and refuses
  the whole restore. Before, both plans were applicable.
- The OpenCode 1.x, OpenCode 2.x, and Pi hosts now quote file names in tool
  text. A path, `old_path`, scope path, unmatched path, changed file, snapshot
  reason, or origin value that holds a control character, a double quote, or a
  backslash prints in double quotes with C escapes, as `git diff` does with
  `core.quotePath=false`. Before, a file named `evil\napplicable: yes` printed
  as two lines in `agent_snap_restore_plan` and `agent_snap_diff` text, and an
  agent could read the second line as a plan or diff fact. Every other name
  prints unchanged, including spaces and non-ASCII text. The JSON results and
  the `details` payloads are unchanged.
- `agent-snap` now runs every Git command with `LANGUAGE=C`, so Git prints
  the messages that the store matches in English. Before, under a locale such
  as `de_DE.UTF-8` and a Git built with translations, a held ref lock failed
  with Git's translated text instead of the named lock error. The store did
  not retry a failed object write. In a reftable repository, a lost
  compare-and-swap failed the create instead of retrying it. `LC_ALL`,
  `LC_CTYPE`, and `LANG` stay the caller's, so a filter sees the same
  character encoding as before.
- `snapshot.list` skips an item ref whose name is not a snapshot identifier.
  A create that reuses the latest snapshot reports only a well-formed
  identifier. Before, a ref planted under `refs/agent-snapshots/` with U+2028
  or NEL in its name listed under that name, and the hosts printed it raw in
  list text. A skipped ref does not count toward `limit`. The TypeScript
  client now rejects a create, list, get, diff, or restore plan result whose

  the field. A list validation error now starts with `snapshot.list result`

  returns a result for a method the client has no validator for. It used to
  return that result unchecked. Error responses are unchanged, so an unknown
  method still rejects with `SnapRpcError` code `-32601`.
- `@agent-snap/opencode` supports OpenCode 2.x as well as 1.x. The entry is
  now one default export, `{ id, server, setup }`: OpenCode 1.x calls
  `server`, OpenCode 2.x calls `setup` and loads it through the new
  `./server` export. On 2.x the plugin follows `session.created`,
  `session.idle`, `session.status`, and `session.deleted` through the event
  stream, registers the same four tools with JSON Schema input, and resolves
  a missing `cwd` from the calling session. Enable it with
  `"plugins": ["@agent-snap/opencode"]` on 2.x; 1.x configuration is
  unchanged. The named `AgentSnapPlugin` export is gone.
- `@agent-snap/pi` accepts Pi Coding Agent 1.x. The peer range was
  `^0.84.0`, which npm reads as `< 0.85.0`; it is now `>= 0.84.0 < 2.0.0`.
  No extension API the plugin uses changed between 0.84 and 1.4.
- `SnapClient` now works in Bun hosts on Linux and macOS. In a compiled Bun
  host, `process.execPath` is the host's own CLI, so the supervisor never
  started and every request failed with `agent-snap supervisor exited
  (code=1, signal=none)`. The OpenCode CLI rejects `--eval` the same way. On
  plain Bun, every `close()` took about 6 s and ended in a SIGKILL, because
  Bun's `net.Socket` never reads the supervisor's control pipe. A host
  executable that re-runs its own entrypoint now fails closed instead of
  starting copies of itself.
- Development uses Bun 1.4: `bun install`, `bun run build`, `bun run test`.
  `bun.lock` replaces `package-lock.json`. `bun run test:node` runs the core
  and Pi tests on Node, and pack-check runs its consumer check on Node and
  Bun. Published packages and their runtime floors are unchanged.
- Read-only snapshot diff (Phase 3): JSONL `snapshot.diff`, CLI
  `agent-snap diff <from> <to>`, `SnapClient.diff`, the OpenCode and Pi
  `agent_snap_diff` tools, and the Pi `agent-snap-diff` command. A diff pages
  through the changed files and hunks between two snapshots of one worktree,
  at most 200 files and 64 KiB of hunks per page by default (`offset`,
  `max_patch_bytes` from 1 KiB to 1 MiB). It runs in a private scratch
  repository that reads the real objects, so Git attributes and configuration
  cannot hide or reshape a change, and the same pair gives the same result
  with the same Git.
- `SnapLike` gains a required `diff` method. Custom `SnapLike`
  implementations must add it.
- Read-only snapshot lookup (Phase 2): JSONL `snapshot.get`, CLI
  `agent-snap get <id>`, `SnapClient.get`, the OpenCode and Pi
  `agent_snap_get` tools, and the Pi `agent-snap-get` command. Lookup
  returns the snapshot detail object (commit, tree, parent, parent
  snapshot id, changed files capped at 1000) and adds error code
  `-32001` for a snapshot that does not exist in the worktree.
- `SnapLike` gains a required `get` method. Custom `SnapLike`
  implementations must add it.
- Snapshot origin (Phase 2): `snapshot.create` takes optional `source` and
  `host`, stored as `Agent-Snap-Source` / `Agent-Snap-Host` lines at the end of
  the snapshot commit message and returned by create, list, and get. The CLI
  records `source: cli`. OpenCode and Pi record their host and lifecycle event,
  `tool`, or `command`. No session identifiers are stored.
- `SnapLike.create` and `SnapClient.create` take an optional fourth `origin`
  argument. `SnapClient` retries without origin when a 0.1.0 binary rejects
  it, so upgrading a plugin before its binary does not stop snapshots.
- `snapshot.create` now rejects, with `-32602`, a reason that contains a NUL
  byte or ends with a paragraph of `Agent-Snap-` lines. Git always refused NUL
  bytes, so 0.1.0 failed such a create with `-32603`, or silently reused the
  latest snapshot when the tree was unchanged. 0.1.0 stored a reason ending in
  `Agent-Snap-` lines as given; this release reads such a snapshot back with
  an origin and a shorter reason.
- `agent-snap` removes the scratch directory of a request that is cancelled
  by SIGTERM or SIGINT. Before, the binary died at once on the teardown
  signal that `SnapClient` sends on timeout, abort, and `close()`. Every
  aborted create left `agent-snap-index-*/index` in the temporary directory.
  Every aborted restore plan also left `evidence.git`, whose private object
  directory can hold blobs of working-tree files. The binary now cancels the
  request in flight, stops its Git children, removes the directory, and
  exits. SIGKILL and Windows `taskkill /F` still run no cleanup. See
  docs/DIAGNOSTICS.md.
- `snapshot.create` fails within about a second when a snapshot ref lock
  stays held. Before, a `latest.lock` or item lock that no process held made
  every later create retry until the client timed out. Git leaves such a lock
  when it dies inside its ref transaction, for example after `kill -9`. The
  `-32603` error names the lock file by its path in the Git directory and says
  to remove it only when no `agent-snap` or Git process is running. Blink
  never removes the lock itself. Creates that contend with each other still
  succeed. See docs/DIAGNOSTICS.md.
- `snapshot.create` retries a snapshot ref directory that a concurrent
  `git pack-refs --all --prune` removed. `git gc` and `git maintenance` run
  that command. Since the stale-lock fix above, such a create failed with
  `update refs: … unable to create directory for`. Blink now retries that one
  failure, for at most 5 attempts with 150 ms of waits in all. A permission
  failure prints the same message and still fails the create after the
  fifth attempt. Every other ref lock failure apart from a held lock still fails at once.
- `snapshot.create` and `snapshot.restore_plan` run no repository hook and
  no fsmonitor program. Before, a create ran the repository's
  `post-index-change` and `reference-transaction` hooks, each hook that
  configuration defines with `hook.<name>.command`, and the `core.fsmonitor`
  program. Each hook received Blink's scratch index. A `post-index-change`
  hook that printed text made the create fail, because the text became part
  of the tree ID. `snapshot.get` also ran the fsmonitor program. Every Git
  command now passes `core.fsmonitor=`. Every command of a create or a plan
  also passes `core.hooksPath` set to an empty directory in its scratch
  directory, and `hook.<name>.enabled=false` for each configured hook. A
  hook whose name contains `=` cannot be turned off that way, so a create
  or a plan in that repository fails with `-32603` and names the hook. The
  captured tree is unchanged.
- `agent-snap` now reads every object ID, ref record, and path from Git's
  standard output alone. Before, the store read the tree ID, the commit ID,
  and the `HEAD` and latest snapshot IDs from Git's standard output and
  standard error together. A clean filter that printed to standard error on
  success failed the create with
  `git commit-tree "<filter text>\n<oid>" ...: not a valid object name` when
  a file was modified in the same second as the scratch index or had a
  modification time in the future. A Git failure message still carries
  Git's standard error. A configured hook listing that is not
  `hook.<name>.<key>` now fails the create or the plan with `-32603`.
  Before, it ended the process with a Go panic. The captured tree is unchanged.
- A failed Git command in `agent-snap` now keeps only the last 8 KiB of its
  standard error. Before, the store kept all of it. A required clean filter
  that wrote 8 MiB of control characters to standard error and failed made
  `snapshot.create` answer with an 8 MiB message on a 50 MB JSONL line. The
  message is now under 9 KiB and the line under 64 KiB. A cut message starts
  its standard error with `[<n> earlier bytes of standard error omitted]`.
  The diff and restore runners kept the first 4 KiB and now keep the last
  8 KiB too. The captured tree is unchanged.
- `SnapClient` now refuses to select the restore entry of a later release.
  The constructor copies `serveArgs` into a frozen array and throws a
  `TypeError` when an element starts with `restore` after its leading `-`
  characters, such as `--restore` or `-restore=1`. It reads the value by index
  and calls no method of it, so a subclass, a Proxy, or an own `map` cannot
  change the copy. A value that is not an array, or that holds a hole or a
  non-string element, throws a `TypeError`. Every spawn checks the copy again. `SnapClient.request` rejects with a `TypeError` for a method that is
  not a primitive string and for `snapshot.restore`. No release of
  `agent-snap` dispatches `snapshot.restore` yet, so no working client
  changes.
- The READMEs and the npm package descriptions name the product Blink. The
  `agent-snap` executable, the `@agent-snap/*` packages, the JSONL methods,
  the `refs/agent-snapshots/` refs, and every host tool and command keep
  their names, so no configuration needs an edit. `docs/NAMESPACE.md`
  records that decision, with install and rollback commands.
- `snapshot.create` of an unchanged tree now records a new snapshot when no
  item ref that lookup accepts points at the commit that `latest` names.
  Before, every such create failed with `-32603` and
  `snapshot ref not found` until a file changed. Deleting a tampered item ref
  with `git update-ref -d`, as the diagnostics advise, led there. The new
  snapshot has the same tree, its parent is the old `latest` commit, and the
  next unchanged create reuses it. No item ref is recreated or deleted.
  A reuse also skips an item ref that lookup refuses. Before, it could report
  such a ref when its name sorted first, and `snapshot.get` then refused that
  id.
- `snapshot.create`, `snapshot.restore_plan`, and `snapshot.list` now read
  objects with replace objects disabled. After Blink resolves the repository,
  every Git command that it runs there passes the resolved `--git-dir` and
  `--work-tree`. A replace ref for `HEAD` no longer changes the tree that
  `create` records, and no longer makes a plan list an ignored file as a
  `delete`. A replace ref for the latest snapshot commit no longer makes
  `create` reuse a snapshot whose tree differs from the working tree. Blink
  takes the Git directory from `cwd`, so a `core.worktree` inside another
  repository no longer sends snapshots there. `docs/COMPATIBILITY.md` says what
  this means for existing snapshots.
- `serve` now rejects a request that holds a key other than `id`, `method`, and
  `params`, with `-32602` and `unknown request key: <key>`, and the method does
  not run. Before, it ignored such a key and read `METHOD`, `ID`, or `Params` as
  the lowercase key, although `docs/COMPATIBILITY.md` said unknown request keys
  are rejected. `SnapClient` has only ever sent those three keys, so hosts see
  no change. A hand-written client that sends another key, such as `jsonrpc`,
  now gets this error and must drop the key.

## Phase 5 — Confirmed Restore

**GitHub:** [#5](https://github.com/deneuv34/agent-snap/issues/5) · [milestone](https://github.com/deneuv34/agent-snap/milestone/6)

**Objective:** Restore selected snapshot content only after an explicit, informed confirmation.

**Design:** [docs/RESTORE.md](RESTORE.md) and FR-16 in [docs/BLINK_SPEC.md](BLINK_SPEC.md). RESTORE.md lists the Phase 5 pull requests in landing order, each with its check.

### Deliverables

- Confirmed full-tree and path-scoped restore operations.
- Clear final result describing source snapshot, safety backup, modified paths, conflicts, rollback outcome, and any manual follow-up.
- Host-specific confirmation UX that cannot be triggered by normal automatic lifecycle events.

### Work items

1. Implement restore writes through a narrowly scoped core API; do not expose raw Git commands directly through host plugins.
2. Enforce the validated dry-run plan at the protocol boundary, and the person's confirmation in the hosts and the CLI ([docs/RESTORE.md](RESTORE.md)).
3. Apply the documented preservation and conflict rules; refuse rather than overwrite anything outside the approved plan. Git's own check before the write is not a complete guard, so the write keeps the window between Git's check of a path and its write as short as Git's own checkout keeps it, and refuses when the repository's configuration changed during the restore ([docs/RESTORE.md](RESTORE.md#the-write-is-a-two-way-read-tree)).
4. Provide an abort and recovery path that references the newly created safety snapshot. A cancel, a timeout, or a host that exits before the write writes nothing. A cancel or timeout after the write starts waits for the write to end and returns its real outcome. Recovery is a new plan toward the snapshot, or a restore of the safety snapshot that records its own backup first. The write runs where no terminal or teardown signal reaches it ([docs/RESTORE.md](RESTORE.md)). The cancellation fix in #31 landed first, as `4e8817e`.
5. Add end-to-end tests that prove no unrelated files, index entries, refs, or worktrees are modified.

### Exit criteria

- No restore path can execute without an explicit confirmation and a verified safety backup.
- Integration tests cover success, cancellation, conflict, partial failure, and recovery.
- The operation has a documented, tested rollback/recovery story.

## Phase 6 — Retention, Observability, and Operational Maturity

**GitHub:** [#7](https://github.com/deneuv34/agent-snap/issues/7) · [milestone](https://github.com/deneuv34/agent-snap/milestone/7)

**Objective:** Make Blink maintainable for long-lived repositories and teams.

**Design:** [docs/RETENTION.md](RETENTION.md), and FR-17 and FR-18 in [docs/BLINK_SPEC.md](BLINK_SPEC.md). RETENTION.md lists the Phase 6 pull requests in landing order, each with its check. Blink never deletes a snapshot ref on its own.

**Scope default (gate `g-retention-scope`, the operator can change it):** Phase 6 delivers a read-only retention report, storage and `git pack-refs` documentation, runbooks, and one confirmed delete that drops one whole snapshot namespace. Selective retention by age or count waits for an operator decision to stop chaining snapshots. [docs/RETENTION.md](RETENTION.md) lists the alternatives with their measured costs. A selective cleanup frees no disk while `latest` stays. An archive move frees nothing. Unchaining frees disk per snapshot but changes FR-2, FR-6, and the meaning of `parent` in section 8.2.

### Deliverables

- Configurable retention and garbage collection for hidden snapshot refs. Under the scope default, this is the namespace drop followed by `git gc --prune=now`, and selective retention is deferred.
- Structured diagnostics/metrics for snapshot latency, deduplication, failures, restore outcomes, and cleanup failures. Under the scope default, Phase 6 carries only the cleanup part. The drop result, its record, and the runbooks report drop failures. Metrics for snapshot latency, deduplication, create failures, and restore outcomes are deferred to an operator decision, and Phase 6 adds no event or metric.
- Documented storage and privacy behaviour.

### Work items

1. Define retention policy inputs: age, count, storage size, per-worktree handling, and protected/manual checkpoints. Under the scope default, the only input is one namespace that a person picks from the report. Age, count, size, and protection rules are deferred with selective retention.
2. Implement a dry-run garbage-collection report before any ref deletion capability. This is the read-only `snapshot.retention_report` (FR-17). It lists every namespace in the repository and lands in every layer before the drop.
3. Add a confirmed cleanup command/API with explicit deletion reporting. This is the CLI `drop` command (FR-18). No JSONL method deletes a ref. A person types a random code on the terminal, and the drop writes a record of every ref it deletes before Git starts. It refuses while a restore holds the worktree's restore lock, and it needs Git 2.30 or later.
4. Add privacy-preserving observability that records operation metadata, not source contents or secrets. The drop result and its record hold ref names, object IDs, counts, and Git's status, and the existing [docs/DIAGNOSTICS.md](DIAGNOSTICS.md) rules cover the rest. [docs/RETENTION.md](RETENTION.md) says why Phase 6 adds no event, and which metrics wait for an operator decision.
5. Define support runbooks for stuck child processes, corrupt refs, failed cleanup, and large repositories. [docs/RETENTION.md](RETENTION.md) lists the rows that `docs/DIAGNOSTICS.md` gains.

### Exit criteria

- Retention cannot delete a protected checkpoint or a ref outside Blink's namespace. Under the scope default, Phase 6 has no protected checkpoints. Retention deletes only a whole namespace that a person confirmed, and only refs under it that the report read.
- Operators can diagnose failures without accessing developer source code.
- Storage behaviour and cleanup safety are documented and tested.

Prioritize work in this order:

1. Safety or data-loss risk.
2. Reliability and cross-platform correctness.
3. Evidence and review quality.
4. Explicit restore capability.
5. Branding, packaging, and operational enhancements.

## 1. Purpose

Blink protects AI-assisted software-development sessions by recording safe, inspectable checkpoints of a Git working tree. It gives developers a trustworthy timeline of the changes an agent made, without modifying the repository's branch history, `HEAD`, real Git index, or working tree during snapshot creation.

Blink is designed to make agent work reversible and reviewable. The current MVP provides safe capture and discovery; intelligent review and restore are planned product capabilities and are explicitly not implemented yet.

## 2. Problem Statement

Coding agents can make many changes rapidly, often across an existing uncommitted working tree. Developers need to:

- preserve the exact pre-agent state before work begins;
- capture meaningful settled states during an agent session;
- identify what changed between checkpoints;
- recover confidently from an unwanted change without corrupting unrelated work;
- use the capability from the coding-agent environments they already use.

Normal Git commits are not sufficient for this purpose: committing affects the user's history and index, while copying files does not preserve Git's tree semantics or integrate naturally with repository inspection.

## 3. Product Principles

1. **Zero impact by default.** Creating or listing a Blink checkpoint must not move `HEAD`, change a branch, stage files in the user's real index, or write working-tree files.
2. **Safety before convenience.** Any future operation that writes to a working tree must be deliberate, validated, previewable, and recoverable.
3. **Git-native storage.** Checkpoints are Git commits and trees held behind hidden refs, not a separate copy of the repository.
4. **Agent-native integration.** Checkpoints are created at session lifecycle boundaries and are available as explicit agent tools and commands.
5. **No silent loss.** Timeout, cancellation, shutdown, and concurrency behaviour must fail closed rather than permit a late or ambiguous operation.
6. **Repository isolation.** Worktrees, repositories, and inherited Git environment variables must not redirect checkpoint storage or cause cross-repository interference.

## 4. Scope

### 4.1 Current MVP (implemented)

- Create a snapshot of a Git working tree.
- List snapshots for a repository, newest first.
- Look up one snapshot by identifier and inspect its commit, tree, parent, and changed paths.
- Compare two snapshots and page through their changed files and hunks.
- Preview a restore of all or selected paths, one page at a time, without writing anything. FR-15 specifies this. The Store, protocol, client, CLI, and both hosts build the plan.
- Record which host integration and which event or action asked for each snapshot.
- Expose a CLI and a long-running JSONL protocol server.
- Provide a type-safe TypeScript client for the Go core.
- Integrate automatic and manual snapshot creation with OpenCode and Pi Coding Agent.
- Deduplicate snapshots when the resulting working-tree tree is unchanged.
- Isolate refs per Git worktree and update the latest pointer atomically.

### 4.2 Planned capabilities (not implemented)

- Confirm a restore, require its safety backup, and apply it. FR-15 specifies the backup rule, and FR-16 specifies the confirmation and the write. Phase 5 builds them.
- Retention and garbage-collection policy.
- Blink naming beyond documentation and package descriptions. [NAMESPACE.md](NAMESPACE.md) keeps every shipped name and lists what a later rename needs.

### 4.3 Non-goals for the MVP

- Replacing Git branches, commits, stashes, or code review.
- Synchronizing snapshots to a remote service.
- Capturing files excluded by Git ignore rules.
- Editing Git history, rebasing, merging, or staging user changes.
- Restoring files automatically or without an explicit user action.

## 5. Users and Primary Workflows

### 5.1 Developer starting an agent session

1. The agent integration identifies the session repository directory.
2. Blink creates a baseline snapshot before, or immediately after, the session starts according to the host's lifecycle semantics.
3. The developer continues working normally; Blink does not alter their branch, index, or files.

**Success condition:** the baseline is discoverable later and represents the Git-visible working tree at the session boundary.

### 5.2 Developer allowing an agent to complete work

1. The host reports that the agent has settled or become idle.
2. Blink coalesces bursty idle/settled events for 1.5 seconds.
3. Blink creates one checkpoint for the stable state unless the agent becomes busy again or the session shuts down.
4. If the tree is identical to the latest checkpoint, Blink reports the existing snapshot as reused.

**Success condition:** routine agent event bursts do not create redundant checkpoints.

### 5.3 Developer creating a named manual checkpoint

1. The developer or agent invokes the create tool/command with an optional reason.
2. Blink records the current tree and returns a snapshot identifier, commit ID, reason, creation time, changed files when newly created, and deduplication status.

**Success condition:** the user can mark a meaningful boundary such as `before refactor` without affecting normal Git state.

### 5.4 Developer inspecting checkpoints

1. The developer or agent invokes the list tool/command for a repository.
2. Blink returns up to the requested number of snapshots in descending creation order.
3. The caller selects a snapshot identifier and invokes the get tool/command to see its commit, tree, parent, and changed paths.
4. The caller can pass two identifiers to the diff tool/command to see the changed files and hunks between them.
5. The caller can use the returned commit and tree IDs with normal read-only Git inspection commands where appropriate.

**Success condition:** the checkpoint timeline is usable without exposing hidden refs as normal branches or asking the caller to construct ref paths.

### 5.5 Future: developer reviewing and restoring

The target Blink experience is:

1. Select a checkpoint or a pair of checkpoints.
2. Inspect a clear file-level and content-level diff.
3. Choose a full-tree or path-scoped restore.
4. Preview the exact writes and conflicts.
5. Confirm the operation after Blink creates a safety backup of the current state.
6. Apply the restore atomically where possible and report the outcome.

This workflow is a product requirement for the restore release, not an MVP behaviour.

## 6. Functional Requirements

### FR-1: Repository resolution

- Every core operation accepts a working directory (`cwd`).
- Blink resolves the repository root with Git, rather than trusting the caller's directory structure.
- Blink resolves the Git directory from `cwd` and the top level with `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`. When `core.worktree` is set, the top level is the directory it names, and the Git directory is still the one that `cwd` finds. Every later Git command in the repository passes both as `--git-dir` and `--work-tree`, so a `core.worktree` that names a directory inside another repository never sends a command to that repository.
- Operations fail with a clear error when `cwd` is not inside a Git repository.
- Git environment variables inherited from the host process are removed for every Git invocation so the resolved repository remains the target.

### FR-2: Snapshot creation

- The operation MUST represent the state that `git add -A -- .` would place in a Git index rooted at the resolved repository.
- Capture and the FR-5 comparison MUST read objects with Git replace objects disabled. A `refs/replace` entry for `HEAD` cannot change the recorded tree, and one for the latest snapshot commit cannot make a create reuse a snapshot whose tree differs from the working tree.
- `.gitignore` MUST be honoured.
- The operation MUST support repositories with and without an existing `HEAD` commit.
- If no nonblank reason is supplied, the stored reason is `manual`.
- The operation MAY receive origin values (`source`, `host`) and stores them as defined in FR-13.
- New snapshot commits MUST use the latest Blink snapshot as their parent when one exists; otherwise, they MAY use the current `HEAD` as parent.
- The operation MUST return the snapshot object defined in section 8.
- Every object ID, ref record, and path list that Blink reads from Git MUST come from Git's standard output alone. A clean filter, a process filter such as Git LFS, or Git itself can print to standard error while a command succeeds, and that text MUST NOT change or fail the create. Blink reads standard error only to report or classify a failed command.

### FR-3: No-impact capture safety

- Snapshot creation MUST use a private temporary `GIT_INDEX_FILE`.
- The temporary directory MUST be outside the target repository, including after symlink resolution, so Blink's own scratch files cannot be captured.
- Scratch files MUST be removed when the operation completes, fails, or is cancelled.
- The binary MUST treat SIGTERM and SIGINT as cancellation of the request in flight. It stops that request's Git children, removes the request's scratch directory, and then exits. A second signal ends the process at once. SIGKILL and a Windows forced termination run no cleanup, so a scratch directory can remain after them.
- The CLI `drop` command is the exception. FR-18 defines how it handles stop signals.
- Snapshot creation MUST NOT write the real Git index, modify `HEAD`, update user branches, or modify working-tree files.
- Capture and create MUST run no repository hook and no fsmonitor program. A hook would receive the scratch index, and an fsmonitor answer would decide which files Git reads. Once Blink has resolved the repository, every Git command it runs there passes `core.fsmonitor=` with an empty value, which turns the fsmonitor off on every supported Git. Every Git command of a create or a restore plan also passes `core.hooksPath` naming an empty `hooks` directory in the operation's scratch directory, and `hook.<name>.enabled=false` for each hook that configuration defines with `hook.<name>.command` or `hook.<name>.event`.
- Blink lists the configured hook names once per create or plan, from every configuration scope, with `git config -z --get-regexp '^hook\..*\.(command|event)$'`. A name is the text between `hook.` and the last `.` of the key. A name that contains `=` cannot be named in `-c`, so the operation fails with `-32603` before it captures anything. The message is `list configured hooks: hook name "<name>" contains '=', so it cannot be disabled on the Git command line`. A hook added to the configuration after the listing can still run, like any other program the repository configures.

### FR-4: Hidden, worktree-scoped storage

- Blink MUST store checkpoint refs below `refs/agent-snapshots/` until the product namespace is formally migrated.
- The namespace MUST be derived from the resolved absolute Git directory, so linked worktrees do not share a checkpoint timeline accidentally.
- A linked worktree's timeline MUST start when Git added that worktree. The start is the modification time of the `commondir` file in the worktree's Git directory, which Git writes once, in `git worktree add`. A main worktree has no `commondir` file, so its timeline has no start.
- A worktree added under a removed worktree's name gets that worktree's Git directory and derives the same namespace. A snapshot whose identifier, compared at its full nanosecond precision, holds a time before the start belongs to the removed worktree and is outside the timeline. Listing skips it (FR-7), lookup does not find it (FR-12), and a create neither reuses it nor chains onto it (FR-5). Deciding this MUST write nothing. Its refs stay until a person drops the namespace (FR-18).
- A snapshot is stored at `refs/agent-snapshots/<namespace>/items/<snapshot-id>`.
- The newest snapshot is stored at `refs/agent-snapshots/<namespace>/latest`.
- The implementation MUST reject symbolic refs at either target path and use `git update-ref --no-deref`.

### FR-5: Deduplication

- Before creating a commit, Blink MUST compare the newly generated tree with the latest snapshot tree.
- If they are identical and an item ref that FR-12 lookup accepts points at the latest commit, Blink MUST return that snapshot with `reused: true` and MUST NOT create a duplicate commit or snapshot ref.
- If they are identical and no such item ref exists, Blink MUST create a new snapshot of that tree whose parent is the latest commit, and move `latest` to it as FR-6 requires. This covers a deleted item ref and one that FR-12 lookup refuses. Blink MUST NOT recreate, repoint, or delete an item ref to avoid it. The next create of the same tree reuses the new snapshot.
- If a new commit is created, it MUST return `reused: false` (omitted from JSON is equivalent to false in the current wire format).
- A `latest` that names a snapshot outside the worktree's timeline (FR-4) counts as no latest for the comparison and for the new commit's parent, so the parent is `HEAD`. The create still moves `latest` with compare-and-swap against the value it read (FR-6).

### FR-6: Concurrent creation

- Updates to the per-worktree item ref and `latest` ref MUST occur in one Git ref transaction.
- Moving `latest` MUST use compare-and-swap against the observed prior value.
- If another create wins the race, the operation MUST re-read state and retry rather than overwrite the other snapshot.
- Git waits up to one second for a snapshot ref lock (`core.filesRefLockTimeout`). When the lock is still held after that wait, the create fails with `-32603` and the message `snapshot ref lock <ref>.lock in the Git directory stayed held for 1s; remove it only when no agent-snap or Git process is running in this repository`. It creates no ref.
- Blink MUST NOT remove, rename, or rewrite a ref lock file, because it cannot tell a lock that a dead Git left from one that a live Git holds.
- A concurrent `git pack-refs --all --prune`, which `git gc` and `git maintenance` run, can remove a snapshot ref's directory between Git's `mkdir` and its lock. Git then prints `cannot lock ref '<ref>': unable to create directory for <path>`. Blink retries only that failure. It makes at most 5 attempts and waits 10, 20, 40, and 80 ms between them. A permission failure on that directory prints the same message, so after the fifth attempt the create fails with `-32603` and a message that starts `update refs:`. It creates no ref.
- Every other `cannot lock ref` failure apart from a held lock, such as a directory/file name conflict with an existing ref, a permission failure on the lock file, or a non-directory in the way, fails the create at once with `-32603` and a message that starts `update refs:`. It creates no ref.
- Blink tells a lost compare-and-swap, a held lock, and a removed ref directory apart by Git's English messages. It runs every Git command with `LANGUAGE=C`, so a Git built with GNU gettext prints them in English whatever the caller's locale. It keeps the caller's `LC_ALL`, `LC_CTYPE`, and `LANG`, so a clean or smudge filter sees the caller's character encoding. A filter also sees `LANGUAGE=C`.
- The resulting snapshot-parent chain MUST remain linear per worktree.

### FR-7: Snapshot listing

- Listing MUST return an empty list when no snapshots exist.
- The default list limit is 20.
- JSONL callers may request an integer limit from 1 through 100; the CLI requires a positive integer.

- Listing MUST skip an item ref whose name is not a snapshot identifier (FR-12). A skipped ref does not count toward the limit. A create that reuses the latest snapshot (FR-5) reports it under an item ref name that passes the same check.

- Listing and that reuse lookup MUST read objects with Git replace objects disabled and parse only Git's standard output, never its diagnostics, as FR-12 lookup does. A warning about an item ref whose name Git cannot read MUST NOT hide or rename a real snapshot.

2. **Preflight:** Blink computes the FR-15 plan again immediately before writing, and refuses when it is not applicable or no longer matches the plan the user saw. FR-16 steps 3 to 8 do this.

If full atomicity is impossible, the result clearly identifies completed and failed paths and offers recovery from the safety snapshot. FR-16 refuses before the first write, runs the write where no teardown signal reaches it, and lists each planned path at its target, at its current side, or at neither in the restore result object. ## 11. Intelligent Review Requirements (Future)

Snapshot diff is implemented as FR-14 and is the evidence layer for review.

An intelligent review layer may prioritize risky changes, summarize scope, and flag likely regressions. It must cite every conclusion with an FR-14 citation and must never replace the source evidence. This repository ships no review generator. The agent that calls the diff tool is the reviewer.

## 13. Delivery Milestones

Deliver the current Go core, protocol, Node client, OpenCode adapter, and Pi extension with the safety requirements in this specification.

### Milestone B: Blink naming and distribution

Brand the user-facing documentation as Blink without breaking existing integrations. [NAMESPACE.md](NAMESPACE.md) records the decision. Add snapshot selection and diff APIs, then present evidence-backed change summaries in supported agent hosts.

Implement the restore safety contract in section 10, beginning with dry-run and backup-only flows before enabling confirmed writes.

Add configurable retention, garbage collection, observability, and policy controls while preserving ref isolation and non-destructive defaults.

These decisions need product and engineering agreement before their related milestones begin:

- Settled: `refs/agent-snapshots/` remains the namespace, with no `refs/blink/` and no migration layer. See [NAMESPACE.md](NAMESPACE.md).
- Which host environments are first-class after OpenCode and Pi Coding Agent.
- Whether review intelligence is local-only, host-provided, or supported by an optional service.

- Versioning for the Blink product release. [NAMESPACE.md](NAMESPACE.md) settled the package names and the executable aliases. The packages stay `@agent-snap/*`, and the executable stays `agent-snap` with no `blink` alias.
- Whether `snapshot.restore_plan` takes a flag filter, so that the confirmation prompt gets the entries flagged `unstaged` or `untracked` and the others from one capture instead of up to 5 pages. It changes FR-15.
- Whether FR-15 blocks a planned path, or a parent of one, whose name holds LF or CR. That keeps prompts short and keeps a path name from forging a line of Git's messages. FR-16 no longer reads those messages, so it does not depend on the block.
- Whether `snapshot.restore_plan` reports a held restore lock, by opening the lock file without creating it and testing a shared lock. Hosts could then say that a restore is running before they record a backup, and Pi could keep automatic snapshots paused until an orphaned write ends. It changes FR-15, so it waits for the CLI step of Phase 5.
