## CLI

Executable name: `agent-snap`.

| Command | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `create [reason] [--cwd <dir>]` | Create one snapshot with source `cli` and no host, and print a snapshot JSON object. `--reason` and a positional reason are mutually exclusive. |
| `list [--cwd <dir>] [--limit <n>]` | Print `{"snapshots":[...]}` newest first. |
| `get <id> [--cwd <dir>]` | Print the snapshot detail object. A missing snapshot fails with `snapshot not found: <id>`. |
| `diff <from> <to> [--cwd <dir>] [--offset <n>] [--max-patch-bytes <n>]` | Print one page of the diff result object. `--offset` is 0 through 2147483647 and `--max-patch-bytes` is 1024 through 1048576. |
| `restore-plan <id> [--cwd <dir>] [--path <path>]... [--offset <n>] [--current-tree <oid>]` | Print one page of the restore plan object. `--path` may repeat, and with none the plan covers the whole tree. `--offset` is 0 through 2147483647 and needs `--current-tree` when above 0. `--current-tree` is a lowercase object ID. It exits `0` when it prints a plan, including one that is not applicable. A missing snapshot fails with `snapshot not found: <id>`, and a `--current-tree` the working tree no longer captures to fails with `working tree changed since the plan`. Both exit `1`. It writes nothing. |
| `ping` | Print `{"status":"ok","version":"<version>"}`. |
| `version` | Print the version string and a newline. |
| `serve` | JSONL server on stdin/stdout. Takes no arguments. |

Missing `--cwd` defaults to the process working directory. CLI failures print
`agent-snap: <error>` on stderr and exit `1`. They are not JSON-RPC errors.

## JSONL protocol

`agent-snap serve` reads one JSON request per line and writes one JSON response
per line. Empty lines are ignored. The server continues after a request-level
error. Maximum request line size: **4 MiB**.

Request:

```json
{"id":1,"method":"snapshot.create","params":{"cwd":"/path/to/repo","reason":"why"}}
```

The server rejects unknown keys on the request or in `params` with `-32602`. A
request holds only `id`, `method`, and `params`, spelled exactly. Any other key
gets `unknown request key: <key>` with the request's `id`, and the method does
not run. A key in `params` that the method does not take gets
`unknown param: <key>`.

A 0.1.0 binary ignores an unknown request key and reads `METHOD` as `method`.
`SnapClient` has only ever sent those three keys, so it behaves the same against
either binary.

`cwd` is required and must be a non-empty string for `snapshot.create`,
`snapshot.list`, `snapshot.get`, `snapshot.diff`, and `snapshot.restore_plan`.

| Method | Params | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ping` | none | `{"status":"ok","version":"<version>"}` |
| `snapshot.create` | `cwd`, `reason?`, `source?`, `host?` | snapshot object |
| `snapshot.list` | `cwd`, `limit?` | `{"snapshots":[...]}` |
| `snapshot.get` | `cwd`, `id` | snapshot detail object |
| `snapshot.diff` | `cwd`, `from`, `to`, `offset?`, `max_patch_bytes?` | diff result object |
| `snapshot.restore_plan` | `cwd`, `id`, `paths?`, `offset?`, `current_tree?` | restore plan object |

`limit` is an integer from **1 through 100**. Omitted `limit` uses the store
default of **20**, newest first.

`id` must match `<YYYYMMDD>T<HHMMSS>.<9 digits>Z-<12 lowercase hex>`. It is
checked before the repository is resolved, and it resolves only inside the
`cwd` worktree's own namespace.

### Error codes

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `-32700` | Parse error (malformed JSON or oversized line) |
| `-32601` | Method not found |
| `-32602` | Invalid params (unknown key, missing/blank `cwd`, bad types, bad `limit`, malformed snapshot `id`, `from`, or `to`, bad diff `offset` or `max_patch_bytes`, bad restore plan `paths`, `offset`, or `current_tree`, `offset` above 0 without `current_tree`, invalid origin value, a reason that contains a NUL byte or ends with an origin paragraph) |
| `-32603` | Internal error (repository resolution, Git, scratch index or evidence repository, ref update, tampered snapshot ref, missing object, a diff that fails its integrity check) |
| `-32001` | Snapshot not found: a well-formed `id`, `from`, or `to` with no snapshot in this worktree |
| `-32002` | Stale restore plan: `snapshot.restore_plan` got a `current_tree` that the working tree no longer captures to |

Error messages name the operation. They must not include working-tree file
contents.

### Snapshot object

| Field | Type | When present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | string | always |
| `commit` | string | always |
| `reason` | string | always |
| `created_at` | RFC 3339 string | always |
| `source` | string | when the snapshot stores an origin source |
| `host` | string | when the snapshot stores an origin host |
| `changed_files` | string array | create of a new snapshot |
| `reused` | boolean | create; `true` when the latest checkpoint was reused |

`id` is `<UTC timestamp>-<first 12 characters of commit>`. List results include
`id`, `commit`, `reason`, and `created_at`, plus `source` and `host` when stored.
`changed_files` and `reused` are create metadata and are not guaranteed on list.
A reused snapshot reports its own stored origin, not the origin of the request.

### Snapshot detail object

Returned by `snapshot.get` and `agent-snap get`.

| Field | Type | When present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id`, `commit`, `reason`, `created_at` | as in the snapshot object | always |
| `source`, `host` | as in the snapshot object | when stored |
| `tree` | string | always |
| `parent` | string | when the snapshot commit has a parent |
| `parent_id` | string | when the parent is a snapshot in the same worktree |
| `changed_files` | string array, at most 1000 entries | always (may be empty) |
| `changed_files_truncated` | boolean | `true` when more than 1000 paths changed |

### Diff result object

Returned by `snapshot.diff` and `agent-snap diff`. FR-14 and section 8.4 of
[`BLINK_SPEC.md`](BLINK_SPEC.md) define every field and rule.

| Field | Type | When present |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `from`, `to` | `{id, commit}` | always |
| `offset` | integer | always |
| `next_offset` | integer, greater than `offset` | when the page does not finish the diff |
| `totals` | `{files, additions, deletions}` over the whole diff | always |
| `files` | array of at most 200 file entries | always (may be empty) |

Each file entry has `status` (`added`, `deleted`, `modified`, `renamed`,
`type_changed`), `path`, `additions`, `deletions`, `patch` (`full`,
`truncated`, `deferred`, `binary`), and `hunks`. It adds `old_path` and
`similarity` for a rename, `old_mode`/`old_oid` unless added,
`new_mode`/`new_oid` unless deleted, `patch_bytes` on some truncated files,
and `lossy: true` when non-UTF-8 bytes were replaced. Each hunk has
`old_start`, `old_lines`, `new_start`, `new_lines`, an optional `section`,
and `text`.

A page lists files from `offset`, default 0. `max_patch_bytes`, default 65536,
bounds the hunk bytes on the page. A diff runs in a scratch bare repository
outside the worktree that reads the repository's objects through
`objects/info/alternates`. Git configuration, attribute files, and replace
refs do not change the result, and the diff writes nothing to the repository.

Mixed versions: a binary without `snapshot.diff` answers `-32601`. So does a
binary without `snapshot.restore_plan`. `SnapClient`, the CLI, and the host
tools expose that method.

A core that carries `restorePlan` needs a binary that answers
`snapshot.restore_plan`. Against an older binary, only `restorePlan` and the
`agent_snap_restore_plan` tool reject. The tool fails with
`SnapRestorePlanUnsupportedError`.
The new `SnapRestorePlanUnsupportedError` export is additive, and
`instanceof SnapRpcError` still matches. `SnapLike` gains a required
`restorePlan` method, so an outside implementation must add it. `-32002`
reaches callers as a plain `SnapRpcError`.

### Snapshot origin

`source` names what asked for a snapshot and `host` names the integration that
sent the request. Both are optional on `snapshot.create` and must match
`^[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*$`, at most 64 characters. Origin is reported by
the caller and is never evidence. Callers must not put session, user, machine,
or path identifiers in it.

A snapshot with origin stores it at the end of its commit message:

```text
agent-snap: <reason>

Agent-Snap-Source: <source>
Agent-Snap-Host: <host>
```

Without origin, the message is the 0.1.0 form, `agent-snap: <reason>`. The
exact parse rule, and the rule that refuses a reason which would read back as
origin, are FR-13 in [`BLINK_SPEC.md`](BLINK_SPEC.md).

Invalid input fails with `-32602` and one of these messages:

- `param must be an origin value: source` / `: host`
- `param must not contain a NUL byte or end with an origin paragraph: reason`
- `param must be a string: <key>` for a non-string value, including `null`

Mixed versions:

- A 0.1.0 binary rejects `source` and `host` with `unknown param: <key>`.
  `SnapClient` then retries the create once without them, logs the drop once,
  and refuses to retry a reason containing `\n\nAgent-Snap-`. A plugin
  upgraded ahead of its binary keeps taking snapshots, without origin.
- A 0.1.0 client ignores `source` and `host` in results.
- A 0.1.0 reader shows a newer snapshot's origin lines as part of its reason.
- A 0.1.0 snapshot whose reason ends with `Agent-Snap-` lines reads back with
  an origin and a shorter reason.

## Hidden Git refs

Namespace: `refs/agent-snapshots/`. Callers never construct these paths; only
`internal/snapshot.Store` owns them. Refs are per worktree. Capture, list, get,
and diff never move `HEAD`, write the real index, or write the working tree;
get and diff also write no refs or objects.

### Replace refs and `core.worktree`

After 0.1.0, every Git command that Blink runs in a repository reads objects
with replace objects disabled. A repository with `refs/replace/` entries sees
four changes:

- `snapshot.create` records the real `HEAD` and working tree. In 0.1.0, a
  replace ref for `HEAD` could add, remove, or change paths in the recorded
  tree.
- `snapshot.create` reuses the latest snapshot only when its real tree
  matches. In 0.1.0, a replace ref for the latest commit could make it reuse
  a snapshot whose tree differed from the working tree.
- `snapshot.restore_plan` reads the real `HEAD`, so its `current_tree` matches
  what `create` now records. In 0.1.0, it could list an ignored file as a
  `delete`.
- `snapshot.list` reports each snapshot's own reason, origin, and creation
  time. In 0.1.0, it reported those of a replacement commit.

A snapshot that 0.1.0 made under such a replace ref keeps the tree it
recorded. That tree can differ from the working tree of that moment. `get`,
`diff`, and `restore_plan` read its commit and tree as stored, as they did in
0.1.0. The first `create` after the upgrade compares the real trees, so it can
record a new snapshot where 0.1.0 reused one. A repository without replace
refs sees no change.

Blink now takes the Git directory from `cwd` and passes it and the top level
to every later Git command. When `core.worktree` names a directory inside
another repository, 0.1.0 wrote snapshots into that other repository's refs
and recorded its whole tree. Now Blink writes into the repository that `cwd`
finds and records the directory that `core.worktree` names, as `git add -A`
in that repository would. When `core.worktree` names a directory outside any
repository, 0.1.0 failed with `resolve object format`, and now the create
succeeds. Snapshots that 0.1.0 wrote into the other repository stay there.
They use the namespace of that repository's own Git directory, so they appear
in its own timeline.

### A reused worktree name

Git names a linked worktree's directory inside the Git directory after the last
part of the worktree's path, and removing the worktree frees that name. In
0.1.0, a new worktree under a freed name derived the same namespace and
inherited the removed worktree's snapshots. Now a linked worktree's timeline
starts when Git added it (FR-4). In such a worktree:

- `snapshot.list` leaves out the removed worktree's snapshots.
- `snapshot.get`, `snapshot.diff`, and `snapshot.restore_plan` answer `-32001`
  for them.
- `snapshot.create` neither reuses them nor chains onto them. The worktree's
  first snapshot has `HEAD` as its parent.

No ref, namespace, method, field, or error code changes. The older refs stay
until a person drops the namespace, and the retention report counts them. A
0.1.0 binary still lists them, and snapshots from both binaries chain onto each
other. A worktree that never reused a name sees no change.

The start is the modification time of the `commondir` file in the worktree's
Git directory. If that time moves forward, as when a backup is restored without
its file times, or the clock steps back past the worktree's creation, Blink
hides the worktree's snapshots until the time is set back. On a file system
with one-second timestamps, a snapshot taken in the second that the name was
reused stays visible.

## OpenCode plugin (`@agent-snap/opencode`)

Supports OpenCode 1.x (`@opencode-ai/plugin` >= 1.18.18) and 2.x
(`@opencode/plugin` >= 2.2.5). Install in `opencode.json(c)`:
`{ "plugins": ["@agent-snap/opencode"] }` on 2.x,
`{ "plugin": ["@agent-snap/opencode"] }` on 1.x.

The package entry (also exported as `./server`) has one default export,
`{ id: "@agent-snap/opencode", server, setup }`. OpenCode 1.x calls `server`
and 2.x calls `setup`; each host imports only its own adapter. The 1.x
adapter loads `@opencode-ai/plugin`, whose `effect` dependency the 2.x
runtime refuses to load from a plugin's `node_modules`, so 2.x never imports
it. On 2.x, tools that omit `cwd` use the calling session's directory, and
the plugin's cleanup ends its event subscription before the shutdown barrier.

OpenCode runs the plugin on its bundled Bun. On Linux and macOS the client
starts its teardown supervisor through the host executable
(`process.execPath`) with `BUN_BE_BUN=1`, which a compiled Bun host honors
from Bun 1.2.16. Against an older host the supervisor fails to start and every
request fails closed.

| `session.deleted` | Cancels that session's work. |
| `agent_snap_create(reason?, cwd?)` | Manual create. |
| Origin | Host `opencode`; source `session-start`, `session-idle`, or `tool`. |
| `agent_snap_list(cwd?, limit?)` | Manual list. |
| `agent_snap_get(id, cwd?)` | Describe one snapshot. Read-only. |
| `agent_snap_diff(from, to, offset?, max_patch_bytes?, cwd?)` | One page of the diff between two snapshots, as Git evidence text. Read-only. |
| `agent_snap_restore_plan(id, paths?, offset?, current_tree?, cwd?)` | One page of the restore plan for a snapshot, as Git evidence text. Read-only. Needs a binary that answers `snapshot.restore_plan`. Applies nothing. |

# Operational diagnostics

Use this when a snapshot operation or client teardown fails. Collect enough to
see *which* operation failed. Do **not** log working-tree file contents, diffs,
secrets, or full file listings.

## What is safe to record

- Operation (`create`, `list`, `diff`, `restore-plan`, `ping`, `close`, teardown)
- JSON-RPC error code and the error message returned by the core
- Repository *existence* / "not a git repository", never file bodies
- Snapshot id, commit id, reason string, `reused`, origin `source` and `host`
- Process id, process-group id, `taskkill` exit status, timeout duration
- Host event name (`session.created`, `agent_settled`, …)
- Binary path (`AGENT_SNAP_BIN`) and protocol version

## What must not be recorded

- File contents, patches, `snapshot.diff` hunks, or `git show` / `git diff` output
- Secrets, tokens, `.env` values, or credential helpers
- Entire `git status --porcelain` dumps in shared logs (path names in a
  short error are acceptable; do not attach the tree)
- Scratch-index file bodies

The Go store wraps Git failures as `git <args>: <error>: <stderr>`. Treat
that stderr as a Git *status* string (paths, ref names). Do not add the
blob or working-tree payload to host logs. A Git built with GNU gettext
prints its own messages in English whatever the locale, because the store
runs Git with `LANGUAGE=C`. The stderr also holds what a clean or process
filter printed, in the filter's own language. The store reads every value
from Git's standard output and discards what a filter prints during a
command that succeeds. The store keeps the last 8 KiB of a failed command's
stderr, because Git prints its own message after any filter output. When
the stderr was longer, it starts with
`[<n> earlier bytes of standard error omitted]`.

| `SnapProtocolError` beginning `snapshot.retention_report result` | The binary and the client disagree about the retention report | Report it as a bug with the Git and `agent-snap` versions. |
| `SnapProtocolError` ending `has a malformed id`, `has a malformed parent_id`, `has a malformed from.id`, `has a malformed to.id`, `has a malformed snapshot.id`, `has a malformed oldest.id`, or `has a malformed newest.id` | The binary returned a snapshot id that does not match the FR-12 format. An older binary can list a planted or corrupt item ref's name, or a Git warning about it, as an id. | Upgrade the binary. Inspect `git for-each-ref refs/agent-snapshots` for the bad ref name. |
| `SnapRestorePlanUnsupportedError` | `restorePlan`, or the `agent_snap_restore_plan` tool, got `-32601` from a binary that predates `snapshot.restore_plan` | Upgrade the binary or set `AGENT_SNAP_BIN`. |
| `SnapRetentionReportUnsupportedError` | `retentionReport` got `-32601` from a binary that predates `snapshot.retention_report` | Upgrade the binary or set `AGENT_SNAP_BIN`. |
| `agent_snap_restore_plan` fails with `-32002` | The working tree changed since the page's `current_tree` | Call the tool again from offset 0 without `current_tree`, then use the new `current_tree` for later pages. The tool only plans and changes nothing. |
| `agent_snap_restore_plan` fails with `-32602` and `missing required param: current_tree` | The call set `offset` above 0 without `current_tree` | Pass the `current_tree` that the first page named, or start again from offset 0. |
| `agent-snap: working tree changed since the plan` from `restore-plan` | `--current-tree` no longer matches what the working tree captures to | Run `restore-plan` again without `--current-tree` and use the new `current_tree` for later pages. The command only plans and changes nothing. |
| `agent-snap: invalid --path: …` or `--offset above 0 requires --current-tree` from `restore-plan` | The flags break the FR-15 scope or paging rules | Fix the flags. The command rejects them before it resolves the repository. |

A failed create must not leave an unobserved checkpoint. If the client
timed out or aborted, assume teardown started and do not trust a late
stdout snapshot.

## Teardown failures

Timeout, abort, crash, and `close()` all start teardown immediately and
fail closed.

### POSIX (Linux, macOS)

The client spawns a guardian supervisor as the process-group leader. It
never signals a bare PGID from the host process (the guardian is in that
group and a recycled PGID must not be signalled).

- `agent-snap supervisor exited (code=1, signal=none)` right after start, in
  a compiled host — the host executable did not run the supervisor script.
  OpenCode needs to be built with Bun 1.2.16 or later.
- `agent-snap supervisor cannot start: this host's executable ran its own
  entrypoint …` — the host re-ran itself instead of the supervisor script and
  refused to start another copy. Fail closed.

Failure messages:

- `failed to inspect agent-snap process group <pid>: …` — `kill(-pgid, 0)`
  returned something other than ESRCH (for example EPERM). Fail closed.
- `agent-snap process group <pid> did not terminate within the verification window` —
  members remained after the grace + wait window.

Check: the binary still running, leftover `git` children, whether the
guardian reported `child-exit` or `spawn-error`. Do not dump the child's
JSONL transcript (it can include `cwd` and reasons only; still keep it
off shared logs if it may contain path lists).

### Windows

Cleanup succeeds only when **both** are true: `taskkill /T /F` reported
success **and** the root process exited.

Failure messages:

- `taskkill failed for agent-snap (pid <pid>): the process tree may still be running`
- `agent-snap (pid <pid>) did not terminate within the Windows tree-cleanup window`
- `agent-snap (pid <pid>) exited before its process tree could be terminated on Windows; descendants may still be running`

A root that exits by itself is **not** success; descendants can survive it.
Check Task Manager / `tasklist` for leftover `agent-snap.exe` or `git.exe`
started by that tree. Record pid and `taskkill` status only.

### Scratch directories left after a hard kill

Each create, diff, and restore plan works in one private directory named
`agent-snap-index-*`. It lives in the system temporary directory (`TMPDIR`
on POSIX, `TMP` or `TEMP` on Windows). When that directory resolves inside
the repository, Blink uses the user cache directory or `/tmp` instead. A
create directory holds a scratch `index` and an empty `hooks` directory,
which a restore plan directory also holds. A diff or restore plan directory
also holds `evidence.git`. A restore plan's `evidence.git/objects` can hold
blobs of working-tree files, so treat a leftover directory as file contents.
Do not attach it to a report.

On POSIX the guardian sends SIGTERM to the process group. `agent-snap`
cancels the request in flight and sends SIGTERM to its Git child, so Git
removes its own ref lock files. When its Git child still runs 500 ms later,
`agent-snap` kills that child. It kills no filter that Git started.
`agent-snap` then removes the directory and exits. The guardian sends SIGKILL
to the group `KILL_GRACE_MS` (2 seconds) later, which ends a filter that
ignored SIGTERM. A directory that is still being removed
then stays behind, in part or in full. A restore plan over a working tree
with tens of thousands of new or changed files can need that long.
A SIGKILL sent straight to `agent-snap` also leaves its directory.

On Windows, `taskkill /T /F` ends the process tree with no cleanup. Every
request that times out or is aborted on Windows leaves its directory.

Blink does not sweep these directories, because it cannot prove that a
directory is not in use by another running `agent-snap`. Delete
`agent-snap-index-*` directories by hand when no `agent-snap` process is
running.

# Namespace decision

**Status:** Decided for Phase 1 ([#1](https://github.com/deneuv34/agent-snap/issues/1)).

Blink is the product name. It appears in documentation and in npm package
descriptions. Every name that a configuration, a script, or a repository
stores keeps the value that 0.1.0 shipped. No release renames these names,
adds an alias for them, or writes a second copy under a new name.

This record is the published migration policy that
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) and [COMPATIBILITY.md](COMPATIBILITY.md) refer to.
Its policy is that nothing migrates.

## The names that stay

| Name | Value | What depends on it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Executable | `agent-snap` | `SnapClient.defaultBin()` looks it up on `PATH`. `AGENT_SNAP_BIN` settings and scripts call it. |
| Override variable | `AGENT_SNAP_BIN` | Host environments that point at a binary outside `PATH`. |
| npm packages | `@agent-snap/core`, `@agent-snap/opencode`, `@agent-snap/pi` | OpenCode `plugin` and `plugins` entries, `pi install npm:@agent-snap/pi`, and the Pi direct placement that nests `node_modules/@agent-snap/core`. |
| JSONL methods | `ping`, `snapshot.create`, `snapshot.list`, `snapshot.get`, `snapshot.diff`, `snapshot.restore_plan` | Every `SnapClient` version. None of them carries a product name. |
| Hidden refs | `refs/agent-snapshots/<worktree>/items/<id>` and `refs/agent-snapshots/<worktree>/latest` | Every snapshot already taken. These refs are the only thing that keeps a snapshot commit reachable. |
| Snapshot commit message | `agent-snap: <reason>`, with `Agent-Snap-Source` and `Agent-Snap-Host` lines | Every 0.1.0 and later reader that parses origin (FR-13). |
| Host tools and Pi commands | `agent_snap_*` tools and `agent-snap-*` commands | Agent prompts, permission rules, and session transcripts that name them. |

## Refs stay under `refs/agent-snapshots/`

The ref namespace is invisible in normal use. It never appears in
`git branch`, and no user types it. A rename buys no brand value and puts
every stored snapshot at risk.

| Alternative | Why it loses now |
| --- | --- |
| Dual-write `refs/blink/` and `refs/agent-snapshots/` | A create would move two `latest` refs. Any binary that writes only one namespace, such as 0.1.0 on another tool's `PATH`, makes the two chains diverge. `list` then has no single truth, and deduplication against `latest` picks a side. |
| Move refs to `refs/blink/` | A 0.1.0 binary lists only `refs/agent-snapshots/`, so every moved snapshot disappears from its `list`. If the move deletes the old refs, a move that stops partway leaves commits that no ref names, and `git gc` can prune them. Git keeps no reflog by default for refs outside `refs/heads/`, `refs/remotes/`, and `refs/notes/`, so nothing else keeps those commits. |
| Read both namespaces, write the new one | Same divergence as dual-write as soon as an older binary writes, and it needs the retention rules that Phase 6 owns before any old ref can go. |

A later move needs all of these first:

- A revision of this record that names the new namespace and the release that starts it.
- A `list` and `get` that read both namespaces and return one chain.
- Compatibility tests that run the old and the new binary against the same repository and show that no snapshot disappears from either `list`.
- A rule that no release deletes an old ref until Phase 6 retention owns deletion.

## A reused worktree name keeps its namespace

**Decided for Phase 5, landing step 8a.**

`git worktree add` names a linked worktree's directory after the last part of
its path, and removing the worktree frees that name. A new worktree under the
name gets the same Git directory, so it derives the same namespace, and the
removed worktree's refs are still there. FR-4 starts each linked worktree's
timeline when Git added it, and a snapshot from before that moment is outside
the timeline. The namespace, its derivation, and the ref layout stay as they
are, so nothing migrates.

| Alternative | Why it loses now |
| --- | --- |
| Salt the namespace with a per-worktree value | Every linked timeline moves unless new code reads both namespaces. A 0.1.0 binary keeps writing the old namespace, so the chains diverge as they do under dual-write. |
| Write an ownership marker on create | No marker exists yet, so the first run cannot tell a live worktree from a reused one. It adds a ref outside the layout above, or a second Blink file in the Git directory. |
| Refuse until a person drops the namespace | Automatic checkpoints stop in that worktree. |
| Delete or move the old refs when the reuse is detected | No release deletes an old ref until Phase 6 retention owns deletion, and a person must confirm a drop. A move is a migration. Git has no hook for worktree removal. |

## The executable stays `agent-snap`, with no `blink` alias

| Alternative | Why it loses now |
| --- | --- |
| Ship a `blink` alias next to `agent-snap` | `SnapClient` never looks for `blink`, so the alias helps no host. It doubles the release binaries and their checksums. The npm package `blink` (version 1.1.42 on 2026-11-04) already installs a `blink` command, and it describes itself as "a tool for building and deploying AI agents". A user with both installed would get whichever comes first on `PATH`. |
| Replace `agent-snap` with `blink` | Every `AGENT_SNAP_BIN` setting that names the old path breaks. Without `AGENT_SNAP_BIN`, every installed `@agent-snap/core` keeps looking for `agent-snap` on `PATH` and fails to start. CLI failures print `agent-snap:` on stderr, and scripts that match it break. |

A later rename needs a minor release that installs both names, a
`SnapClient.defaultBin()` that tries both, and compatibility tests that start
every published host against each name.

## Packages stay `@agent-snap/*`

On 2026-11-04 no `@agent-snap` package is on the npm registry yet. A package
rename costs the least before the first publish, so this is the cheapest
point to change it. The names stay anyway, for these reasons:

- The package names match the executable, the variable, the refs, and the commit message. Renaming only the packages leaves the product with two names in one install.
- A user who already built the packages from source has `@agent-snap/opencode` in `opencode.json` and `@agent-snap/core` in a Pi extension directory. A rename breaks both on the next update.
- AGENTS.md forbids a rename without a published migration policy and compatibility tests, and Phase 1 adds neither.

| Alternative | Why it loses now |
| --- | --- |
| Publish the same code as `@blink/*` too | With two names for one plugin, a host could load both and register every `agent_snap_*` tool twice. Each fix ships twice, in lockstep. |
| Publish `@blink/*` and deprecate `@agent-snap/*` | `npm deprecate` warns every current install. The Pi direct placement imports `@agent-snap/core` by name, so it breaks until the user rebuilds it. |

Versions follow [RELEASE.md](RELEASE.md). No `@agent-snap` package is
deprecated.

- An `@agent-snap/` or `@blink/` package that it did not pack.
- An `agent-snap` or `blink` command that the built binary does not list in its usage text, or a subcommand that the usage text does not list. # Restore design

**Status:** Accepted. Phase 4, [#4](https://github.com/deneuv34/agent-snap/issues/4). Confirmed writes stay disabled until Phase 5, [#5](https://github.com/deneuv34/agent-snap/issues/5).

This record decides what a Blink restore does, and how Phase 4 prepares it without writing a user file. It answers the Phase 4 work items in [`BLINK_DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md`](BLINK_DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md) and shows how the design meets each acceptance requirement in section 10 of [`BLINK_SPEC.md`](BLINK_SPEC.md). The exact wire contract goes into the spec as a new functional requirement after this record is approved.

A developer who wants to undo an agent's work gets a preview that names every path a restore would write or delete, and a safety snapshot of the current state before anyone is asked to confirm. A host developer gets one read-only call that is safe to give an agent, and a write call that agent tools and lifecycle hooks cannot reach. The next maintainer gets one definition of "the current state", shared by capture, the preview, and the backup.

## A restore moves the working tree between two captured trees

Every restore is a move from a current tree to a result tree. Both are trees in the sense of FR-2, the state that `git add -A -- .` would place in an index seeded from `HEAD`.

- The current tree is the tree that `snapshot.create` would capture at that moment.
- For a full-tree restore, the result tree is the snapshot's tree.
- For a path-scoped restore, the result tree is the current tree with every covered path replaced by its version in the snapshot, or removed when the snapshot lacks it.

A restore writes working-tree files only. It never writes the real index, `HEAD`, branches, or normal refs. After a restore, `git status` shows the restored content as unstaged changes against the index. That is the same result as `git restore --worktree --source=<snapshot>`, plus the deletions described in [the state table](#each-repository-state-has-one-response).

Ignored files are outside both trees. A restore never writes, overwrites, or deletes an ignored file. A planned write that would land on one, or replace a directory that still holds one, blocks the plan. A directory whose tracked files the restore deletes keeps its ignored files, because Git removes only empty directories.

## Restore is three operations with one safety class each

| Operation | Safety class | Phase | Does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `snapshot.restore_plan` | Read-only | 4 | Computes the move and every blocker. Writes nothing to the repository. |
| `snapshot.create` with reason `restore backup` | Capture | Shipped | Records the safety backup of the current state. |
| `snapshot.restore` | Working-tree write | 5 | Applies one planned move after a human confirmed it. |

A method name says how much it can change. A validation bug in the plan method cannot become a write, because the plan method has no write path. Every snapshot method today is `snapshot.<verb>`, so the restore methods keep that prefix and put the safety class in the suffix. Only `snapshot.restore` restores.

The roadmap names the dry run "`snapshot.restore`". This record moves that name to the Phase 5 write and calls the dry run `snapshot.restore_plan`. A method called `restore` that does not restore invites a caller to send it expecting a write, or worse, to send the write expecting a preview.

A new method, not a new parameter, carries the plan. A binary older than this work answers `-32601`, and the client reports that restore is not supported by the installed binary. A new optional parameter on an existing method would instead fail as `unknown param` on every older binary.

These shapes were rejected:

- One method with a `mode` or `dry_run` field. It puts three safety classes behind one name and one validator.
- One `prepare` call that creates the backup and returns the plan. It records a checkpoint for every preview, moves `latest`, and lets any agent tool that can preview also write hidden refs. The roadmap requires the dry run to leave the repository unchanged.
- A separate backup method that records only when the captured tree equals the plan. The Phase 5 write checks the backup's tree against the plan anyway, so the extra method would repeat that check at the cost of a protocol method, a `Store` method, a CLI command, and their types.
- A stateful plan held by the server. The CLI is one process per command, and `SnapClient` restarts its transport, so server state would be lost between the plan and the confirmation.

## The plan writes nothing to the repository

`snapshot.restore_plan` captures the current tree with the same steps as `Store.Create`. The steps move into one function that both call. `Create` writes new objects into the real object store. The plan writes them into a private object directory in the scratch directory, which sits outside the repository by the FR-3 rule.

1. Create the private object directory, and write its `info/alternates` file with the real object directory, as `Store.Diff` does for its evidence repository.
2. Run `read-tree HEAD`, or `read-tree --empty` on an unborn branch, then `add -A -- .` and `write-tree`, with a scratch `GIT_INDEX_FILE` and `GIT_OBJECT_DIRECTORY` set to the private directory.

Git runs in the real Git directory, so excludes, `core.excludesFile`, attributes, filters, and line-ending rules are the repository's own. Every step sees the real objects through the alternates file, so the tree ID is the one `Create` would record. The plan hashes every working-tree file, as `Create` does, and writes only the objects the real store lacks.

The guarantee is that the plan adds, removes, or changes no file under the Git directory, and writes no ref, index, configuration, log, or working-tree file. Git refreshes the modification time of an existing object that it would otherwise write again, so a plan can touch the modification time of a loose object or a pack file. That only delays when `git gc` may prune an unreachable object.

The plan runs every program the repository configures for capture, exactly as `Create` does. That includes clean filters, long-running process filters such as Git LFS, and a `core.fsmonitor` hook. Blink cannot control what those programs write. Git LFS, for example, keeps a copy of each file it cleans under `.git/lfs`. The guarantee covers Git and Blink, and the spec will say so.

The plan then compares the current tree with the result tree in a private evidence repository, as `Store.Diff` does, whose alternates list both the real and the private object directories. The scratch directory is removed when the plan finishes, fails, times out, or is cancelled. A cancelled plan returns no result.

Reads of the real index use plumbing under `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0`. `ls-files -z -v -s` reads entries and flags, and `diff-index --cached` finds staged paths. The plan never runs `git status`, which rewrites the index.

These shapes were rejected:

- Hiding the real objects from `add`, so that Git cannot refresh their modification times. On a repository whose `HEAD` holds CRLF content under `core.autocrlf=true`, that capture produced a different tree from `Create`, because Git reads the `HEAD` blob to decide how to convert line endings. The plan and the backup would then disagree.
- Capture inside the evidence repository. That repository has no `info/exclude` and no repository configuration, so its tree differs from what `Create` records.

## The plan lists every path the restore would change

A plan holds the target snapshot (`id`, `commit`, `tree`), the `paths` it covers (absent for a full tree), `current_tree`, `result_tree`, `applicable`, the repository blockers, the unmatched scope paths, totals over the whole plan, and one page of entries.

Each entry names one path and one action, which is `create`, `modify`, `type_change`, or `delete`. It carries the current and target `{mode, oid}`, three flags, and at most one path blocker. The flags compare three trees at that path, so they never depend on file timestamps:

- `staged` when the real index differs from `HEAD`.
- `unstaged` when the current tree differs from the real index.
- `untracked` when the current tree has the path and the real index does not.

Entries come from `diff-tree -r -z --raw --no-renames` in byte order of the path. A restore acts per path, so a rename is a `delete` and a `create`, and rename detection belongs to `snapshot.diff`.

A page holds at most 200 entries, as an FR-14 diff page does, and `next_offset` names the next page. A request for a later page must repeat `current_tree`. Each page captures the working tree again, and if it no longer captures to that tree, the plan fails as stale instead of mixing two states in one listing. A host that shows the totals and the first page pays for one capture. `applicable` is true exactly when there is no repository blocker, no unmatched scope path, and no entry with a blocker.

The plan carries no hunks. After the backup exists, `snapshot.diff <backup> <snapshot>` shows the content of a full-tree move with FR-14 citations. For a path-scoped move, that diff also shows changes outside the selected paths.

## The safety backup is a snapshot of the planned state

The backup is an ordinary `snapshot.create` with reason `restore backup` and source `restore-backup`, made after the plan and before the confirmation. The host shows the backup ID to the user before it asks for confirmation, which is the Phase 4 exit criterion. Phase 4 needs no backup code of its own. Its work is a test that the plan's `current_tree` equals the tree that `create` records right after it, in every state the plan supports.

The backup is valid for a plan when its tree equals the plan's `current_tree`. The Phase 5 write checks that again. If the working tree changed between the plan and the backup, the host plans again. Equality is proven by tree ID, never by origin, which FR-13 says is not evidence.

FR-5 deduplication stays. When `latest` already has the current tree, the backup is that snapshot, reported with `reused: true` and its own reason and origin. Section 10 asks for a "fresh" safety snapshot. This record reads that as a fresh capture whose tree is proven equal to the state before the restore, which a reused commit is. The spec pull request words the requirement that way.

The backup holds the cleaned form of every file, as every snapshot does. After a write that stopped part way or was killed, a file whose clean filter loses bytes holds neither its original bytes nor a copy Blink can return to them (Phase 5 probe obs 8 and 9). Recovery restores the cleaned form from the backup, not the original bytes.

A backup becomes `latest` and the parent of the next snapshot, so the timeline stays linear across a restore. A declined restore leaves its backup in the timeline as an ordinary checkpoint. Nothing marks a reused backup as a backup. Phase 6 decides what retention protects, and until Phase 6 Blink deletes no snapshot.

## A restore is bound to five values, not a token

The Phase 5 write takes `snapshot`, `paths`, `current_tree`, `result_tree`, and `backup`. The core re-derives each one before it writes:

- The backup resolves through FR-12 lookup, and its tree equals `current_tree`.
- A fresh capture of the working tree equals `current_tree`.
- The result tree recomputed from the snapshot and `paths` equals `result_tree`.
- The recomputed plan is applicable.

If any check fails, nothing is written. A plan computed against a different snapshot, scope, or working-tree state cannot be applied. The values are content addresses, so there is no secret, no expiry, and no server state, and a one-process CLI works the same way as `serve`.

These shapes were rejected:

- A core-minted token, such as a nonce or an HMAC. It is returned to whoever called the plan, so an agent that can preview holds it. A one-process CLI would also need key or nonce state on disk.
- A digest over the entry list. `result_tree` already pins the exact move.

# Retention design

**Status:** Proposed, revision 3 with the round-3 review's fix-up. Phase 6, [#7](https://github.com/deneuv34/agent-snap/issues/7). Nothing in this release deletes a snapshot ref.

This record decides how Blink lets a person see and remove snapshot data. It answers the five Phase 6 work items in [`BLINK_DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md`](BLINK_DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md). The wire contract is FR-17 and FR-18 in [`BLINK_SPEC.md`](BLINK_SPEC.md), with the objects in sections 8.7 and 8.8.

A developer gets a read-only report of every snapshot namespace in the repository. The report names the worktree that each namespace belongs to, or says that none does, as for a removed worktree or a moved repository. The developer then gets one terminal command that drops one whole namespace after they type a random code from the prompt. A drop followed by `git gc --prune=now` frees the namespace's objects. The next maintainer gets one read-only method, one CLI command that deletes, and one Git transaction.

Deleting a hidden ref is the first operation that removes Blink data.

## Phase 6 scope is a default the operator can change

The first revision of this record designed a selective cleanup by age and count. Its adversarial review failed it, and the coordinator then applied a default under gate `g-retention-scope`. This revision designs that default.

Phase 6 delivers these by default:

- A read-only retention report (FR-17).
- Documentation of what a snapshot costs on disk and how to reclaim it, including `git pack-refs`.
- Runbooks.
- One confirmed delete. It drops one whole snapshot namespace, which is `latest`, every item, and every other ref under it (FR-18).

Selective retention by age or count waits for an operator decision to stop chaining snapshots. The operator can change the default. The measured choices are in the following table.

| Choice | What it frees | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default. A report and a whole-namespace drop. | Every object of the namespace, after `git gc --prune=now` (drop probe G2, 1284 KiB to 1 KiB). | No selection. A person keeps a whole timeline or drops it. |
| A selective cleanup by age and count, the first revision. | Nothing. Deleting items while `latest` stays kept every object after `git gc --prune=now` in all 8 configurations (round-1 storage probe). | Its one measured gain is a faster ref scan, which `git pack-refs --all` already gives. At 10,001 loose refs, `list` took 1046 and 1428 ms, and 192 to 321 ms once packed (round-1 scale probe). Every snapshot that a 0.1.0 binary wrote has no origin, so its protection rules could never select one. |
| An archive move. Move items to another ref prefix. | Nothing. | Its gain is a shorter `list`, which a person never sees, because `list` already returns at most the newest 100. |
| Unchain new snapshots. A create names `HEAD` as the commit parent and records the previous snapshot in its message. | The deleted snapshot's own objects. Round-1 review measured 1539 KiB to 513 KiB after it deleted four items and ran `git gc --prune=now`. | It changes the MUSTs in FR-2 and FR-6 and the meaning of `parent` in section 8.2. A 0.1.0 binary that reads a new snapshot reports `changed_files` against `HEAD` and no `parent_id`. Snapshots written before the change stay chained and free nothing. |
| No delete in Phase 6. A report and documentation only. | Nothing. | Removed worktrees and moved repositories leave namespaces that nothing in Blink can reach. |

The default beats the selective cleanup because the drop is the only delete that frees disk under chaining, and it needs no selection rules. It also covers the namespaces that removed worktrees and moved repositories leave behind. The default beats unchaining because unchaining changes the parent semantics of every snapshot, which is a spec decision for the operator and not a part of this docs change.

## What a snapshot costs on disk

Each snapshot commit names the previous snapshot as its parent (FR-2, FR-6). `latest` names the newest commit, so `latest` reaches every snapshot of its chain. A namespace that a reused worktree name holds has two chains (FR-4), and only item refs reach the older one. Deleting an item ref while `latest` stays makes no object of that chain unreachable. The round-1 storage probe showed it on Git 2.54 and 2.56, SHA-1 and SHA-256, files and reftable.

A snapshot of text edits is small. Round-1 review recorded 300 snapshots of one-line edits in a clone of this repository, and the packed size grew from 1007 KiB to 1167 KiB after `git gc`, about 0.5 KiB a snapshot. Disk grows fast only when large files that are not ignored keep changing, because every changed blob is stored again.

Dropping a namespace removes every ref that reaches its commits. The drop probe recorded five snapshots with a 256 KiB random file each, then dropped the namespace in all 8 configurations:

- `git gc --prune=now` removed the oldest dropped commit, and the pack went from 1284 KiB to 1 KiB (G2).
- The linked worktree's namespace and its commit stayed (D4, G3).

A plain `git gc` keeps an unreachable object only while it is younger than `gc.pruneExpire`, two weeks by default. Git judges an object in a pack by the age of its pack. The gc-age probe dropped a namespace in all 8 configurations and then ran a plain `git gc`. When the pack had just been written, the oldest dropped commit stayed. When the pack was last written 30 days before, the commit was gone after that one `git gc`. Snapshots that an earlier `git gc` packed are usually that old. So recovery from a drop can end at the next `git gc`, and Git can start `gc --auto` after ordinary commands. That last fact is inferred from Git's documentation, and no probe ran an automatic gc.

A dropped namespace's refs have no reflog (D4), so Git keeps no other record of them.

A long timeline also slows ref scans. A `list`, and a `create` whose tree did not change, read every item ref of the namespace. `git pack-refs --all` packs loose refs into one file. Git's automatic `gc --auto` runs it, because `gc.packRefs` defaults to true. That is inferred from Git's documentation.

## Blink never deletes on its own

No create, list, host event, timer, or other automatic step deletes a snapshot ref. Only the CLI `drop` command deletes, after a person types the prompt's code on the terminal. This is the gate default `g-retention-default`, which the operator can change.

## The report lists every namespace in the repository

`snapshot.retention_report` takes `cwd` and an optional `offset`. It never reads a commit message, so its cost does not depend on reason length.

### The report reads names and values, and types only `latest`

The report runs three reads. Every Git command runs with `LANGUAGE=C`, as on main, so Git's messages are in English.

1. One `git for-each-ref --format='%(refname) %(objectname) %(symref)' refs/agent-snapshots/`. It reads no object.
2. One `git cat-file --batch-check` with the object ID of each listed `latest`. It prints `missing` for an object the repository does not have. It runs with `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1`, because in a partial clone the same command in the real repository fetched a missing object into the real object store (the promisor probe in [`RESTORE.md`](RESTORE.md)). A Git older than 2.44 ignores the variable. That is inferred from the release that added it, and nothing ran on an older Git.
3. `git symbolic-ref -q <latest>` for each namespace whose `latest` the first read did not list and did not name as broken.

Round 2 printed `%(objecttype)` in the first read. The broken-ref probe showed that one ref to a missing object then makes `for-each-ref` exit 128 with `fatal: missing object`, in all 8 configurations. The report failed for every namespace in the repository, and every drop failed with it. Without `%(objecttype)`, `for-each-ref` exited 0 and listed that ref, and the other namespace still reported. `cat-file --batch-check` then printed `<oid> missing` for a `latest` whose object was gone.

A ref that Git ignores is broken. `for-each-ref` skips a ref whose file holds no object ID, prints `warning: ignoring broken ref <ref>` on standard error, and exits 0 (broken-ref probe, files backend). It skips a ref whose name Git rejects, such as `items/a..b` or `items/x y`, and prints `warning: ignoring ref with broken name <ref>` instead (round-3 review, both Gits, SHA-1 and SHA-256). Round 3 counted only the first form. A ref with a rejected name was then never counted, the drop exited 0 and reported `dropped`, and the file stayed. `git gc --prune=now` then failed with `fatal: bad object refs/agent-snapshots/...`. The report counts each line of either form that names a ref under `refs/agent-snapshots/` as a broken ref of its namespace, or in `totals.other` when the name has no namespace. `symbolic-ref -q` on a broken `latest` exited 128 with `fatal: No such ref`.

The report reads the standard error of `for-each-ref` in full, up to 4 MiB, and fails closed:

- Standard error longer than 4 MiB fails the report with `-32603`. The round-3 review measured 36,985 bytes for 400 broken refs, so the bound holds about 40,000 warnings. The report never counts from a cut text.
- Any line that is not one of the two warnings for a ref under `refs/agent-snapshots/` fails the report with `-32603`. A Git that words a warning differently therefore fails the report and refuses the drop, and never yields a false `dropped`.

The Store's shared runner, `output`, keeps only the last 8 KiB of standard error and returns it only when Git fails, so this read collects standard error itself. The report never runs it on a `latest` that the warning named, and it reports a `symbolic-ref` exit other than 0 and 1 as a broken `latest` too. Reftable stores no file that a person can corrupt this way, so the probe ran these cases on files only.

`for-each-ref` also skips a symbolic ref whose target does not exist, and prints no warning (drop probe X4). The third read finds a dangling symbolic `latest`. A dangling symbolic item ref stays invisible to every listing command, and only `git fsck` names it (X4). Blink never writes a symbolic ref, so such a ref exists only when something else wrote it. A runbook row covers it.

A namespace is the 16 lowercase hex digits after `refs/agent-snapshots/` and before the next `/`. A ref whose path does not have that form, such as `refs/agent-snapshots/README` or `refs/agent-snapshots/tmp/x`, belongs to no namespace. The report counts it in `totals.other` and no drop touches it. The broken-ref probe listed both of those example refs without an error.

For each namespace it reports:

- The namespace, and whether it is the namespace of `cwd`.
- The worktree it belongs to, when one does.
- The number of refs, of item refs whose names are snapshot identifiers, and of broken refs. A broken item ref counts as a broken ref and not as a snapshot, whatever its name.
- The oldest and newest of those identifiers and their times.
- The state of `latest`, which is `commit`, `not_commit`, `missing_object`, `symbolic`, `missing`, or `broken`.
- A digest of every ref under the namespace with its value.

### A namespace maps to a worktree through the common Git directory

A worktree's namespace is the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of its absolute Git directory, as `git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir` prints it. Git prints that path with symbolic links resolved. For the main worktree, it is the common Git directory C. For a linked worktree, it is `C/worktrees/<name>`.

The report finds C without `--path-format`, which Git 2.31 added:

1. G is what `git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir` prints in `cwd`.
2. When `G/commondir` exists, C is its content joined to G when it is relative, then cleaned, with symbolic links resolved. Otherwise C is G.
3. The main worktree's namespace comes from C. Each entry under `C/worktrees/` gives the namespace of `C/worktrees/<entry>`.

`git rev-parse --git-common-dir` is not used, because it printed `.git` in the main worktree and `../.git` in its subdirectory. A join of that relative path keeps a symbolic link in the path, such as macOS `/var`, that Git resolved to `/private/var` before it hashed. The mapping probe ran the derivation from the root and a subdirectory of the main worktree, a linked worktree, and a worktree made with `--relative-paths`, in a repository under `/var/folders`. In all 8 configurations it gave exactly the namespaces that `agent-snap create` wrote from each of them.

The report shows a worktree path for each mapped namespace. The main worktree's path is the first `worktree` line of `git worktree list --porcelain`. A linked worktree's path is the directory that holds the `.git` file named by the entry's `gitdir` file. The report reads at most 4096 bytes of that file, only when it is a regular file, and joins a relative path to the entry directory. Git 2.48 and later write a relative path there for `--relative-paths`, and the probe saw `../../../../wtrel/.git`. When the file cannot be read, the namespace still maps and the path is absent. `git worktree list` blocks on an entry whose `gitdir` file is a FIFO, which a FIFO probe showed on Git 2.54 and 2.56 (landing step 2). So the report skips that command when any entry's `gitdir` is not a regular file, and the main worktree then has no path. After `git worktree remove`, the worktree's entry was gone and its namespace stayed (W1).

A new linked worktree that takes a removed worktree's name derives the same namespace. Its timeline starts when Git added it (FR-4), so `list` and lookup leave out the removed worktree's snapshots. The report reads refs, so it counts both timelines under the new worktree, and the drop deletes both. Round-1 review measured the shared namespace. The drop prompt shows the snapshot times, so a person can see that a timeline is older than its worktree.

### The digest covers every ref with its value

The digest is the lowercase hex SHA-256 of one line per ref under the namespace, in ref-name order. A line is the full ref name, a space, a value, a space, the symbolic target or `-`, and a line feed. The value is the object ID the ref resolves to, the zero object ID for a ref that resolves to nothing, or `broken` for a broken ref.

Any create, deletion, or change under the namespace changes the digest. The drop probe saw a create change it (D2).

Both hosts get `agent_snap_retention_report`. Its text lists each namespace's fields under the quoting rule of host tool text. It ends with a line for the person, not an instruction to the agent: "This report changed nothing. A person can drop one namespace from their own terminal with `agent-snap drop <namespace> --digest <digest>`."

## The record is written before anything is deleted

An identifier cannot be rebuilt from its commit. `recordTree` takes the identifier's time from the clock after `commit-tree`, and the commit stores whole seconds. So the drop writes the transaction it will run to a record file before Git starts, and Git reads its transaction from that file. The record holds the ref names, which contain the identifiers, and the object IDs. It holds no reason, path, or file content.

The record is `<user cache directory>/agent-snap/drops/<UTC time>-<namespace>.txt`, where the user cache directory is Go's `os.UserCacheDir`. The Store writes it, because the transaction is Git policy and AGENTS.md keeps Git policy out of `cmd/agent-snap`. The Store creates the directory with mode 0700, checks that it is a directory that the user owns with mode 0700, creates the file exclusively with mode 0600, refuses a path inside the worktree as the scratch rules do, and syncs the file and its directory before Git starts. When any of that fails, the drop exits `1` and deletes nothing. A kill after Git starts leaves the record in place, because Blink never removes it.

Three more paths sit beside the record and share its name up to `.txt`. `<name>.out` and `<name>.err` take Git's standard output and standard error, and `<name>.hooks` is the empty `hooks` directory that `core.hooksPath` names. The Store creates the two files exclusively with mode 0600 and the directory with mode 0700, before Git starts, and never removes them, so Git can still write to them and find no hook after the CLI dies. Step 8 lists the configured hooks once, as FR-3 does for a create, and step 9's Git carries `hook.<name>.enabled=false` for each.

A cache directory is a place that cleaners and backup tools may clear. The record stays there because it serves one recovery soon after a drop, and a `git gc` can end that window anyway. The prompt says both.

The prompt and the result name the record. To recover, a person runs this in a worktree of the repository:

```sh
sed -n 's/^delete \(refs\/agent-snapshots\/[0-9a-f]\{16\}\/[^ ]*\) \([0-9a-f]\{40,64\}\)$/\1 \2/p' <record> |
while read -r ref oid; do git update-ref --no-deref "$ref" "$oid" "" || echo "not recovered: $ref"; done
```

Each ref comes back on its own, only when it does not exist, and only while its object exists. The by-hand probe ran this loop in all 8 configurations:

- After a create had started a new chain, the three dropped items came back beside the new one, and the new `latest` stayed. Round 2's single transaction failed as a whole there with `reference already exists`.
- With one item's object gone, that item failed with `nonexistent object`, and the other items and `latest` came back.
- With `latest` a symbolic ref to `refs/heads/precious`, or a dangling one to `refs/heads/ghost`, the loop left `latest` and every branch unchanged, and created no branch.

A `delete <latest>` line with no old value names no object, so the loop skips it. Recovery cannot bring back a dangling symbolic `latest`.

## Only the CLI drops, after a person types a random code on the terminal

The command reuses the FR-16 CLI rules. It checks that standard input, standard output, and standard error are each the controlling terminal, then opens the terminal, and refuses with exit `4` when any check fails. It has no `--yes`, and it never reads the code from standard input.

The code is six hex digits from `crypto/rand`, made for each prompt and printed only on the terminal. No report, record, tool result, or earlier run holds it. Round-1 review showed why it must not come from the digest. The report tool returns the digest, so an agent could tell the person what to type without the person reading the prompt.

Blink does not claim to stop an agent that has a shell. Such an agent can run Git itself, start its own `serve`, or give the CLI a terminal. Round-1 review measured two ways. A driver built on Python's `pty.fork()` passed every terminal check and typed the code it read from the prompt. A process that inherited the person's controlling terminal pushed input into it with `TIOCSTI` on macOS. The guarantee covers `serve`, host tools, lifecycle hooks, `SnapClient`, and any caller that gives the CLI pipes. [`RESTORE.md`](RESTORE.md) states the same limit for a restore. The random code stops blind injection, because the injector cannot know the code. It does not stop a process that reads the terminal.

The prompt shows:

- The namespace, whether it is the namespace of `cwd`, and its worktree or that no current worktree maps to it.
- The number of refs, of snapshots, and of other refs, the oldest and newest identifier with their times, and the state of `latest`.
- That the timeline can hold the safety backup of a restore, and that dropping it removes that undo.
- The record path, that the system may clear its directory, and that recovery may already be impossible after the next `git gc`, including an automatic one.
- That the drop takes up to a few seconds and the terminal must stay open.
- The code.

Ctrl-C, `SIGTERM`, `SIGHUP`, or `SIGQUIT` at the prompt declines. The drop prints that nothing was deleted and exits `4`. A wrong line, an empty line, or the end of input declines the same way.

The drop refuses on Windows until a Windows CI job runs the terminal cases, as the restore does. That refusal and the Git version check come before the terminal check, so Windows always exits `1`.
